title: 体道
original: 道可道，非常道。名可名，非常名。无名天地之始。有名万物之母。故常无欲以观其妙。常有欲以观其徼。此两者同出而异名，同谓之玄。玄之又玄，众妙之门。
translation: The Tao that can be explained through language cannot be termed the eternal Tao. The name that can be named cannot be called the eternal name. Nothingness is the origin of Heaven and Earth; Being is the Mother of the myriad things. Therefore: One can perceive the Mystery of the Tao by observing Nothingness;One can perceive the manifestations of the Tao by observing Being. Nothingness and Being originate essentially from the same source, but are given different names; They are both called Mystery. Understanding this Mystery leads us to the door of the myriad things.
commentaryZh: 第一章可以看作是《道德经》整部书的前言，是统领全书的概括性总结，提出了“道”的概念。“道”是宇宙万物的总根源，统领万物。《道德经》中“道”的概念显得比较抽象，翻译成英文比较困难，暂且翻译成“Tao”。“道”体现了老子哲学的本体论思想（ontology），即宇宙本源的哲学思想。“道”生成万物，人类的语言与逻辑也是“道”之所生，故，语言与逻辑不可能讲清楚何为“道”。老子提出的“道”也可以理解为“宇宙万物运行的规律”及“自然法则”等等。“无”和“有”可理解为“阴”与“阳”。老子在《道德经》第一章就提出了贯穿整部作品的核心概念：“无”和“有”。这对概念相当于“一阴一阳之谓道”中的“阴”与“阳”的概念，是理解《道德经》灵魂的关键。如：“天下万物生于有，有生于无。”“无”是天地的开始，是创世纪之前的状态，具有先天性特征。“有”是万物的母体，是创世纪之后的状态，具有后天性特征。“无”与“有”各有其作用，相当于一个事物的两个方面，是一体的，互相依赖，不可分割。这对概念涉及对立统一的辩证法思想。世人都对看得到、听得见、摸得着的“有”感兴趣，但对看不到、听不见、摸不着的“无”兴趣不大。但老子会在以后的篇章里告诉我们：“无”的作用更大，所以要“悟道”。一个人如果能够常常站在“无”的角度去理解和观察世界，那他就“玄之又玄”了。“有”可以理解为世人能够具体化的事物或沉迷其中的物质世界，如：有形资产、金钱、地位、权力、名利、美女、豪宅、名车、建筑、文学作品等等；“无”可以理解为存在但我们却看不到、听不见、摸不着的东西或精神世界，如：无形资产、精神、思想、灵魂、信仰、意志、格局、意识形态、心态、气场、心有灵犀、暗 能 量 、暗 物 质（dark matter）、粒 子（particle）、量 子（quantum）及 量 子 纠 缠（quantum entanglement）等等。在翻译“无”与“有”时可以采用哲学概念的“无”（Nothingness）和“有”（Being）的对应英译词汇。
commentaryEn: The first chapter may be regarded as a preface to the entire Tao Te Ching. It serves as a general introduction that sets the conceptual framework for the whole text and introduces the central notion of the Tao. The Tao is understood as the ultimate source of the universe and the principle that underlies and governs all things. It is highly abstract and therefore difficult to translate precisely into English. For this reason, it is often transliterated into “Tao.” It reflects the ontological dimension of Laozi’s philosophy, that is, his inquiry into the ultimate origin of the cosmos. All things arise from the Tao, including human language and logic. Consequently, language and logic fail to describe what the Tao is. It may also be understood as the underlying patterns or natural principles that govern the operation of the universe. Laozi also introduces a pair of concepts which runs throughout the entire work: nothingness and being. These two concepts can be interpreted in relation to the complementary forces of yin and yang, which constitutes Tao. They form a key to understanding the central vision of the Tao Te Ching. For example, Laozi states that “all things in the world arise from being, and being arises from nothingness.” In this framework, nothingness may be understood as the primordial condition preceding the formation of Heaven and Earth. By contrast, being refers to the mother from which concrete things emerge, representing the condition after the formation of Heaven and Earth. Each has its own function and they are like two sides of a single reality, mutually interdependent and inseparable. This relationship reflects a form of dialectical thinking centered on the unity of opposites. People are often more interested in what can be seen, heard, and touched, that is being, and pay less attention to what cannot be directly perceived, that is nothingness. Yet Laozi later suggests that the function of nothingness is in many respects more fundamental, and that genuine understanding of the Tao requires insight into this unseen dimension. A person who is able to approach the world from the perspective of nothingness is said to enter a state of profound insight. In practical terms, being may be associated with tangible things and the material conditions in which people often become absorbed—wealth, status, power, reputation, beautiful women and material possessions, etc. By contrast, nothingness may be associated with intangible yet real dimensions of existence, such as spirit, thought, belief, will, and states of mind. For purposes of philosophical discussion, the pair may be provisionally rendered in English as Nothingness and Being, though neither term fully captures the richness of the original Chinese concepts.

title: 养身
original: 天下皆知美之为美，斯恶矣；皆知善之为善，斯不善已。故有无相生，难易相成，长短相形，高下相倾，音声相和，前後相随。是以圣人处无为之事，行不言之教。万物作焉而不辞。生而不有，为而不恃，功成而弗居。夫唯弗居，是以不去。
translation: Once the people of the world recognize what is beautiful, Then arises the notion of what is ugly; Once the people of the world recognize what is good, Then arises the concept of evil. Therefore: Being and Nothingness inter-depend in terms of growth; The difficult and the easy inter-depend in terms of completion; The long and the short inter-depend in terms of comparison; The high and the low inter-depend in terms of position; Sound and voice inter-depend in terms of harmonious effect; The front and the back inter-depend in terms of company; What is mentioned above is an eternal phenomenon. Therefore: A sage practices non-action and teaches without preaching; The myriad things spring up themselves without his interference; He creates them but does not claim his ownership; He contributes much, but does not boast about that; He accomplishes much, but does not claim credit for that. It is because he chooses to claim no credit for his achievements that they are in no way obscured.
commentaryZh: 本章可以视为《道德经》整部书的目录，也是老子辩证法及相对论哲学思想的概括。老子在这一章提出了一些对立统一及相对论的概念。如：美丑、善恶、有无、难易、长短、高下、音声、前后等等。更多的类似概念在以后的章节还会陆续出现。老子在这一章提出了世间万事万物的概念都是因人的比较而产生的，也就是由人的区别心导致的，而这种因比较而产生的概念也会随时空的变化而变化，故人不可固执于某种固定的认知。另外，老子认为世间万物也是相辅相成、相互依赖（inter-depend）、相互补充（inter-complement）而存在的。 因此，有道的圣人会悟出事物的内在规律，依道而行，不人为干涉万物的自化进程，不违背自然规律，不妄为，也不多为，即行“无为”和“不言之教”；有了功绩不自视功高、不占为己有、不咄咄逼人。而圣人越是谦卑处下，他反倒越会被人民爱戴，他的功绩永远被百姓铭记在心，可谓“死而不亡者寿”。
commentaryEn: This chapter can be regarded as an outline of the entire Tao Te Ching, as well as a concise summary of Laozi’s dialectical and relational mode of thinking. Here, Laozi introduces a series of paired concepts that express the unity of opposites and the relativity of human judgments, such as beauty and ugliness, good and evil, being and nothingness, difficulty and ease, long and short, high and low, sound and tone, and front and back. Similar patterns of thought continue to appear in later chapters. In this chapter, Laozi suggests that many of the distinctions we make about the world arise from comparison, that is, from the human tendency to discriminate and categorize. Because such distinctions depend on perspective, they also shift with changes in time and circumstance. For this reason, people should not cling rigidly to fixed ways of understanding the world. At the same time, Laozi maintains that all things exist in relationships of mutual support and interdependence. Therefore, the sage who follows the Tao comes to recognize the inner patterns governing the world and acts in accordance with them. He does not forcibly interfere with the natural processes through which things transform and develop, does not violate the rhythms of nature, and avoids unnecessary actions. Instead, the sage practices non-action and teaches without excessive words. When accomplishments are achieved, the sage does not claim credit, does not seek recognition, and does not impose authority on others. The more humble and self-effacing the sage remains, the more deeply respected and supported he becomes among the people. His contributions endure in the hearts of the community, and in this sense, he achieves true longevity

title: 安民
original: 不尚贤， 使民不争。不贵难得之货，使民不为盗。不见可欲，使民心不乱。是以圣人之治，虚其心，实其腹，弱其志，强其骨；常使民无知、无欲，使夫智者不敢为也。为无为，则无不治。
translation: A ruler should refrain from honoring the worthy in that it keeps people from contending and infighting endlessly for promotions; A ruler should refrain from prizing the rare objects hard to procure in that it prevents people from committing theft and robbery; A ruler should keep people away from the objects that easily excite people'sdesires so that their minds are far from being tempted. Therefore: A sage should purify people's hearts and meet their basic material needs; He should weaken their selfish desires and keep their bodies fit. In this way people will be kept far away from deceptive knowledge and covetous desires and the deceptively clever will hesitate in doing cunning things solely for their own interests. When non-action is put into practice, nothing is left in disorder.
commentaryZh: 本章是《道德经》中最容易被误读的章节之一。从字面看，仿佛老子在倡导人们不要向“圣贤”和“模范”学习，不要有太多的“想法”和“欲望”，有“愚民”的倾向。但如果我们考虑一下老子所生活的那个极其动荡的历史年代：一个混战迭起、民不聊生的春秋末年，一个各诸侯国为扩大地盘而不择手段、巧取豪夺的昏暗年代，一个弥漫着“春秋无义战”的烽火狼烟的特殊时代……就不难理解老子苦口婆心地劝导要抑制人们，尤其是统治者的贪婪欲望，以及有道的君王应该如何去教化人民祛除贪欲、强健体魄以回归生命本真的这些做法了。在老子看来，超出了人们基本需要的需求就是“欲望”。为满足贪欲，人们就会伪装自己，表现出“高尚”的人格，以获得各种赞美与荣誉并以此来达到自己不可告人的目的。如果人人如此，那么社会就会“大伪”频现，人人为私利争得你死我活，进而导致各种灾难性的“内卷”。所以有道的圣人要行“无为而治”，使人们摆脱贪欲的泥潭以避免无谓的纷争，那样天下才能太平。“无为而治”的核心目的就是控制人们的“欲望”。
commentaryEn: This chapter is one of the most frequently misunderstood passages in Tao Te Ching. At first glance, Laozi may seem to discourage people from learning from sages or exemplary figures and to caution against having too many ideas or desires, an attitude that could even be mistaken for obscurantism. However, if we consider the turbulent historical context in which Laozi lived, an era marked by constant warfare, widespread suffering among the populace, and fierce competition among rival states seeking territorial expansion by any means, it becomes easier to understand his persistent call to restrain excessive desires, especially those of rulers. He was concerned not only with curbing greed, but also with guiding people to free themselves from destructive cravings and to restore a more balanced and healthy way of life. In Laozi’s view, any desire that goes beyond basic human needs becomes a form of excess. In pursuit of such desires, people may disguise themselves, projecting an appearance of moral refinement in order to win praise, honor, and social recognition, while secretly advancing their own self-interest. If such behavior becomes widespread, society will be filled with hypocrisy, and individuals will compete relentlessly for personal gain, leading to escalating conflict and social disorder. For this reason, the sage who follows the Tao governs through non-coercive action in order to reduce excessive desires and prevent needless conflict. Only in this way can social harmony and stability be sustained. The core of this principle lies in moderating selfish desires.

title: 无源
original: 道冲而用之，或不盈。渊兮似万物之宗。解其纷，和其光，同其尘，湛兮似或存。吾不知谁之子，象帝之先。
translation: The Tao is like an invisible and empty vessel, yet its usefulness is inexhaustible.Vast and unfathomable, it seems to be the ancestor of the myriad things. Its usefulness functions when it comes to dulling sharpness, eliminating entanglements, softening brightness and mingling with dust. Invisible and formless, it seems to exist. I fail to know whose son it is, and it seems to have existed before the Emperor of Heaven.
commentaryZh: 本章讲“道”的形态、“道”的作用及“道”存在的“先天性”。“道”像“冲”（也读“盅”），喻指“道”的“空虚、虚空”特性，因为“盅”是一种喝酒的器皿，中间为空，方能盛液体，但“道”的这种因“空”而产生的作用却“不盈”，即“不枯竭”。“道”空冥幽深，仿佛是万物的宗主。“道”的这种“冲虚平和”的作用可以达到“挫其锐，解其纷，和其光，同其尘”的“玄同”之境。这个“冲”字也可以理解为“一阴一阳”相互作用的状态，即“虚而不满”的境界，也就是老子所强调的“天道忌满，人道忌全”的思想源头。在以后的章节，老子还会有更详细的论述。“道”看起来隐而无形，却真实存在。我不知道它是谁的儿子。它好像在天帝之前就已经存在了。
commentaryEn: This chapter discusses the form and function of the Tao, as well as its existence prior to all things. The Tao is compared to an empty drinking vessel to highlight its essential quality of emptiness. Like a vessel that must remain empty in order to be useful, the Tao derives its power precisely from this emptiness. Moreover, its generative capacity is inexhaustible. Profound and unfathomable, the Tao appears to be the source of all things. Through its quiet, balanced, and unobtrusive operation, it brings about a state of deep harmony—softening sharpness, resolving conflict, blending radiance, and merging with the dust of the world. This condition is often described as mysterious unity, a state in which distinctions are reconciled without being forcibly erased. The notion of emptiness can also be understood as the dynamic interaction of yin and yang. It points to a condition of remaining unfilled rather than becoming overfull, a state of balance that avoids excess. This idea lies behind Laozi’s teachings that Tao of Heaven avoids extremes, and that human conduct should likewise resist the pursuit of perfection or completion. Later chapters will elaborate on this principle in greater detail. Although the Tao appears hidden and formless, it nonetheless truly exists. No one can say from where it originates. It seems to have been present even before the highest powers of Heaven came into being.

title: 虚用
original: 天地不仁，以万物为刍狗。圣人不仁，以百姓为刍狗。天地之间，其犹橐迭乎？虚而不屈，动而愈出。多言数穷，不如守中。
translation: Heaven and Earth are impartial, treating the myriad things like useless sacrificial straw dogs; The sage is also impartial, treating the people like useless sacrificial straw dogs. Is the space between Heaven and Earth like a huge bellows? Much as it is empty, with pulling and pushing air will never be exhausted. If driven on, it gives out more air. The fewer orders are issued, the better; It would be more advisable to practice non-action.
commentaryZh: 本章也是最容易被误读的章节之一。从字面上看，老子是一位“不仁”、“冷漠”和没有“怜悯之心”的人。其实，读懂后我们会发现是我们思维的段位太低、认知过于世俗化，因此冤枉了老子。老子讲的“不仁”是指天地对待万物没有分别心、一视同仁、不偏不倚，不会因为你善就对你好，或因为你恶就惩罚你。天地无意志，没有分别心而任万物自然生长。正如荀子所言：“天行有常，不为尧存，不为桀亡。”天地体现着“道”的运行规律，所以没有个人感情色彩。圣人最能体道、悟道，所以在对待百姓时也同样“不仁”。“刍狗”是古代人们祭祀时用草扎成的狗，以其替代实物，用前人们很重视而用完后就扔掉了，任其自生自灭。接着，老子把天地之间比喻成一个巨大的“风箱”，因为风箱中间是空的，如天地之间的虚空一样。这是一个无比生动的比喻，因为只要拉动风箱的杆就会产生无穷无尽的风。这个比喻就是“道”的“虚空”的作用。天地万物依赖“道”这个“大风箱”而生生不息。天下也如同一个大风箱虚而不竭。老子警告统治者要遵循“道”的规律，不要以区别心对待自己统治的天下，应该让万事万物顺其自然生生不息。所以，统治者没有必要整天发号施令去干扰百姓正常的生活，那样会加速国家政权的解体，统治者不如保持虚静，即“守中”，也可理解为“行无为之事”。
commentaryEn: This chapter is among the most frequently misunderstood passages in  Tao Te Ching. On the surface, Laozi may appear unkind, indifferent, and even unsympathetic. Yet, when the text is properly understood, we realize that such misjudgment arises from the limitations of our own thinking and from an overly worldly interpretation of the world. The term “impartial” (a translation of the Chinese term bu ren, which can be misleading if taken literally as “unkind”) does not imply cruelty or a lack of compassion. Rather, it suggests that Heaven and Earth treat all things without partiality—equally and without favoritism or bias. They do not reward goodness nor punish wrongdoing. Possessing no intentional will or personal preferences, Heaven and Earth simply allow all things to grow and develop according to their own nature. As the philosopher Xunzi observed, Heaven follows its constant course and does not change in response to human affairs. Heaven and Earth thus embody the operating patterns of the Tao and are free from personal emotion or preference. The sage is the one who most fully understands and aligns with the Tao, and therefore likewise appears impartial in dealing with the people. The term “straw dogs” refers to ritual objects made of straw that were used as symbolic substitutes for real offerings in ancient ceremonies. Before the ritual, they were treated with great respect; once the ceremony was over, they were simply discarded. Laozi then compares the space between Heaven and Earth to a great bellows. Like a bellows, it is empty at the center, yet capable of generating an endless supply of movement and energy. This is a remarkably vivid metaphor: when the bellows is put into motion, an inexhaustible stream of air is produced. The image illustrates the generative power of the Tao’s emptiness. All things in the universe depend on the Tao—this great “cosmic bellows”—for their continual creation and renewal. The world itself is likewise like a bellows: empty, yet never exhausted.

title: 成象
original: 谷神不死是谓玄牝。玄牝之门是谓天地根。绵绵若存，用之不勤。
translation: The Tao is like the Spirit of the Valley and never dies; It can be called the Mysterious Female. The Door of the Mysterious Female is the root of Heaven and Earth. The Tao seems to last forever and its use remains inexhaustible.
commentaryZh: 在本章中，老子把“道”比喻为“谷神”和“玄牝”，而“玄牝之门”指“雌性生殖器”，也就是生养万物的根源。山谷的特点是“虚空”，而“道”的特点突出表现在“虚空”这一属性上。因此，“道”是无穷无尽、永远“不死”的。“牝”为雌性动物，为生养之所，“玄牝”喻指繁衍万物之母体，故用来比喻“道”。
commentaryEn: In this chapter, Laozi compares the Tao to the “Spirit of the Valley” and the “Mysterious Female.” The “Door of the Mysterious Female” refers to the female generative organ, that is, the source from which all things are born. The defining feature of a valley is its emptiness, and the nature of the Tao is most clearly manifested in this quality of emptiness. For this reason, the Tao is inexhaustible and never perishes. The term Female refers to female beings that generate and nurture life. The Mysterious Female thus symbolizes the maternal source that gives birth to and sustains all things, and is therefore employed as a metaphor for the Tao.

title: 韬光
original: 天长地久。天地所以能长且久者，以其不自生，故能长生。是以圣人後其身而身先，外其身而身存。非以其无私邪！故能成其私。
translation: Heaven and Earth last forever. The reason is justified by the very fact that they do not exist for their own sake. Therefore: The sage puts himself behind others when it comes to fame and wealth, yet puts himself in front of others when he serves the people. It is through selflessness that he ends up achieving what is in his own best interest, isn't it?
commentaryZh: 本章讲天地能够长久存在的根本原因，即天地所做的一切都不是为了自己。这是贯穿《道德经》最重要的思想之一，即利他思想（altruism）。有道的圣人依此天道而为，故能做到全心全意地为人民服务。在利益、地位、名声面前他们主动退后，而面对困难、磨难、灾难，乃至死亡，他们勇往直前而不顾及自己的生命安全。他们这种处处为别人着想而不考虑个人利益得失的大公无私的行为最终也成就了他们最高的理想，即“以至公至至私”。他们一心为公，所以永远被人民爱戴与怀念。
commentaryEn: In this chapter, Laozi explains why Heaven and Earth endure: all that they do is not for themselves. This idea of altruism is one of the central themes running throughout Tao Te Ching. The sage, following this Tao, acts accordingly and is therefore able to devote himself wholly to his people. In matters of gain, status, and reputation, he places himself behind others; yet in the face of hardship, suffering, disaster, and even death, he advances without regard for his own safety. By consistently putting others before himself and disregarding personal gain and loss, he ultimately fulfills his highest ideal. This is what is meant by the saying that “through the utmost selflessness, one attains utmost self-fulfillment.” Precisely because he is wholly devoted to the common good, he is forever cherished and remembered.

title: 易性
original: 上善若水。水善利万物而不争，处众人之所恶，故几於道。居善地，心善渊，与善仁，言善信，正善治，事善能，动善时。夫唯不争，故无尤。
translation: The greatest goodness resembles the virtue of water. W ater nurtures the myriad things but does not claim credit for that; It prefers to stay in lowly places detested by people, and because of this water comes closest to the Tao. Therefore: The sage puts himself behind others when it comes to gains and profits; His heart remains as profound and calm as deep water; He contributes much to the welfare of others without expecting reward; He values trustworthiness both in words and deeds; He practices non-action in governance; He adopts flexibility in handling affairs; He knows well when to choose the right time in doing things. He incurs no blame in that he does not contend for his own interests.
commentaryZh: 本章是《道德经》最著名的章节之一。此章论述了水的“利他”之外的七种接近“道”的“德行”，即“水之七德”：“居善地”“心善渊”“与善仁”“言善信”“政善治”“事善能”“动善时”。一个人若效仿水的以上几种近于“道”的德行，那他就不会有大的过错了。
commentaryEn: This chapter is one of the most well-known in Tao Te Ching. It expounds the seven virtues of water beyond altruism, which approximate the Tao: dwelling in humble places, a mind as calm as deep water, interacting with others benevolently, sincerity in words and deeds, non-action governance, flexibility in doing things, and acting at the proper time. One who models oneself on these virtues of water, which are close to the Tao, will be free from serious fault.

title: 运夷
original: 持而盈之不如其己；揣而锐之不可长保；金玉满堂莫之能守；富贵而骄，自遗其咎。功遂身退，天之道。
translation: Filling the cup below the brim is better than filling it to the brim for water will overflow; An over-sharpened sword cannot maintain its sharpness long for it will be easily dulled. If a man possesses too much wealth, he cannot keep it safe for it will incur theft and robbery. Extravagance and arrogance out of wealth and honor will bring one ruin. Therefore: After achieving success, one should keep a low profile and conceal his brilliance; In fact, such a man acts in accord with the Tao of Heaven.
commentaryZh: 本章主要讲“适可而止”的道理。这个道理对人生的成败极其重要，因为它就是“天道”。老子告诉我们：与其把水杯倒满不如在水杯装满之前适可而止，以防水溢出。刀剑打磨得过于锋利就容易折断。聚敛财货过多是守不住的，因为会受到他人的时刻觊觎，要么被偷盗抢劫，要么被子孙挥霍掉。富贵而骄纵必将招来灭顶之灾，这是自己“妄作”导致的。所以，功成名就后，人要懂得收敛，懂得急流勇退，保持内心对名利和权位的淡泊，不要居功自傲，这样做才是符合“天道”的行为。
commentaryEn: This chapter centers on the principle of knowing when to stop, a principle that is essential for sustaining success and accords with the Tao. Laozi illustrates this through a series of examples: rather than filling a cup to the brim, it is better to stop before it overflows; a blade sharpened to excess is liable to break; and excessive wealth invites the envy of others and cannot be kept. Wealth and honor coupled with arrogance inevitably brings ruin upon oneself, for it arises from his own overreaching. Therefore, once achievement and recognition have been attained, one should know when to withdraw, remain unassuming, and stay detached from fame, gain, and power. Only in this way can one act in accordance with the great Tao.

title: 能为
original: 载营魄抱一，能无离乎？专气致柔，能如婴儿乎？涤除玄览，能无疵乎？爱国治民，能无为乎？天门开阖，能为雌乎？明白四达，能无知乎。
translation: In pursuit of the Tao, can you keep body and soul together? In achieving gentleness, can you concentrate on your breath to border on the tender state of a newly-born child? In cleansing and purifying your inner world, can you manage to be flawless? In governance, can you practice non-action? In terms of sensual contact with the outside world, can you keep soft and calm like a female? In comprehending the world around you, can you do so without using your cunning intelligence? The Tao creates the myriad things and nurtures them; Yet it never claims its ownership; It nourishes them, yet never boasts about it; It heads them, yet never dominates them; This is called "mystic virtue"
commentaryZh: 老子在本章中主要论述了“实体”与“虚体”的辩证关系，主要目的是突出他的“玄德”理念。“玄德”是“道”的显性特征。能否达到“玄德”的境界，要看一个人能否修炼到以下几种境界：灵魂与肉体能否融为一体，持守大道而不分离？聚集精气神能否达到像初生婴儿一样柔顺和谐之至柔？洗涤自己心灵的尘垢能否使内心世界一尘不染？爱民治国能否遵循“无为而治”的原则？调动感官去感知、接触外面世界能否像雌性一样保持内心的平静祥和？了解周围的一切能否不用智巧与心机？生化万物、养育万物并使万物繁衍生息，但不因此将万物占为己有，也不自恃功高并主宰他们，这就是最深远、最玄妙的德行，即“玄德”。
commentaryEn: In this chapter, Laozi explores the dialectical relationship between substance and emptiness, with the aim of elucidating the idea of mystic virtue, which is the manifestation of the Tao. To attain this state depends on a series of forms of self-cultivation. One must be able to unify body and spirit without departing from the Tao, to gather and harmonize one’s vital energies until they become as supple and balanced as those of an infant, and to cleanse the mind so that it remains free from defilement. At the same time, one must be able to govern the country through  non-action, to treat the external world as calmly and softly as a female, and to understand things without relying on cunning intelligence. Ultimately, one should give rise to and nurture all things, allowing them to flourish without possessing them, taking no credit and exercising no domination over them. This is the deepest and most subtle form of virtue, mystic virtue.

title: 无用
original: 三十幅共一毂，当其无，有车之用。埏埴以为器，当其无，有器之用。凿户牖以为室，当其无，有室之用。故有之以为利，无之以为用。
translation: Thirty spokes come together around the hub of a wheel, yet it is the emptiness of the hub that gives the wheel its usefulness. Clay is molded into a vessel, yet it is the emptiness of the vessel that actualizes its usefulness. Doors and windows are made in the walls of a house, yet it is their empty space that makes the house useful. Therefore: People benefit from Being (what they have), yet it is through Nothingness (the emptiness of what they have) that they come to know the function of what they possess.
commentaryZh: 本章侧重论述“无”的作用和价值。三十根辐条共同围绕着把它们固定到 一起的圆木（即轮毂），而轮毂中间必须是空的才能装上车轴，车轮才能转动起来，才有车的作用。和（huó）泥制作陶器，陶器中间必须留出空间才有盛物的作用。建筑房屋，要装门安窗，而门窗及房间中有了空的地方，房屋才有了居住的作用和价值。所以，“有”（车、器皿、房屋的具体存在）给人带来益处的前提是它们“无”（车、器皿、房屋的虚空的存在）的价值。
commentaryEn: In this chapter, Laozi emphasizes the function and value of nothingness. Thirty spokes converge at a hub, yet it is the empty space at the center that allows the wheel to turn and thus perform its function. Clay is shaped into a vessel, but it is the hollow within that makes it useful. Doors and windows are cut into walls to form a room, yet it is the empty space inside the walls that makes the house livable. Therefore, while being (the tangible forms of wheel, vessel, and house) provides practical benefit, it is nothingness ( the emptiness within) that makes such benefit possible.

title: 检欲
original: 五色令人目盲，五音令人耳聋，五味令人口爽，驰骋畋猎令人心发狂，难得之货令人行妨。是以圣人，为腹不为目，故去彼取此。
translation: Too much color dazzles the eye; Too much music deafens the ear; Too much delicious food ruins the appetite; Chasing and hunting excites nervous agitation; Rare and precious objects tempt people to steal and rob. Therefore: The sage chooses to live a simple life, and rejects sensual pleasures.
commentaryZh: 老子在本章中鞭挞了春秋时期统治阶级所过的声色犬马、物欲横流的奢靡生活。他们为了满足感官不断升级欲望，沦落为物欲的奴隶。老子连续用了三个以“五”开头的句子及“驰骋畋猎”和“难得之货”来表达红尘世界的诱惑之多。当然“五”并不是具体的数字，而是表达多的意思。绚丽多彩的颜色令人眼花缭乱，可谓“乱花渐欲迷人眼”；多种音调混杂的音乐会令人失去听觉；味道混杂的食物会让人失去味觉的灵敏度；骑马飞驰狩猎会令人心性放荡不羁；珍奇的货物会勾起人贪婪的欲望，令人失去理性而走上犯罪的道路。所以，有道的圣人只满足于一日三餐的饱腹而不去追逐声色犬马的放荡生活。他们拒绝奢靡的生活而满足于简朴自然的生活。
commentaryEn: In this chapter, Laozi criticizes the indulgent and extravagant lifestyle of the ruling class during the Spring and Autumn period. In their pursuit of sensory pleasure, their desires grow without limit and eventually come to control them. To illustrate the abundance of worldly temptations, Laozi employs a series of parallel images—five colors, five sounds, five flavors, hunting, and rare goods—where “five” signifies multiplicity rather than a precise number. Excessive colors dazzle the eyes; complex and discordant sounds impair hearing; rich and varied flavors dull the palate. Galloping in the hunt leads to restlessness and a loss of self-restraint, while rare and precious goods stir up greed, causing people to lose their judgment and even fall into wrongdoing. For this reason, the sage who follows the Tao seeks only simple living rather than extravagance. Rejecting luxury and indulgence, he is content with a plain and natural way of life.

title: 厌耻
original: 宠辱若惊，贵大患若身。何谓宠辱若惊？宠为下。得之若惊失之若惊是谓宠辱若惊。何谓贵大患若身？吾所以有大患者，为吾有身，及吾无身，吾有何患。故贵以身为天下，若可寄天下。爱以身为天下，若可托天下。
translation: Because people care too much about fame and fortune, they wil feel dismayed whether they are honored or disgraced. How to explain this? He who receives a favor from his superior will feel dismayed when he receives it because such honor is something to be valued and a sign that he is respected by his superior; He who loses such favor wil feel dismayed, too, because this means a kind of disgrace to be terribly feared. Why do I value my life as much as honor and disgrace? Because I have attachment to the ego, which turns out to be the very source oftroubles; Suppose I have no attachment to the ego, what else can distress me? Therefore: If there is someone who cares about the world as much as his own attachment to the ego, he can be entrusted with the task of governing it; If there is someone who loves the world as much as his own attachment to theego, it can be left to his care.
commentaryZh: 在本章中，老子阐释了何为“宠辱若惊”和“贵大患若身”及何种品格的人可以寄托天下。老子在这里指出人性中的弱点之一，即人们特别计较个人得失。人们通常会在得到宠爱或受到冷落羞辱时感到惊恐，他们察觉到自己得宠或受辱，都如同察觉到自己身患重疾一样惊恐不已。因为受宠的人处于下位，处于被动地位，所以被上位的人宠爱会感到不安，而一旦失去宠爱也会惊恐万分，沮丧不已，这就是“宠辱若惊”。我之所以有忧患，是因为我有这个身体，因为它会生病或因无法预料的不幸而受到严重伤害；假如我没有这个身体，我还担心有什么祸患吗？所以，能把天下和自己的身体看得一样珍贵的人，才可以付之以治理天下的重任；能把天下当成自己的身体一样爱惜的人，才可以付之以天下苍生。这样的人一定是有道的君主。本章强调破除“自我”，放下我执与私欲，以无私之心奉献天下，方能超脱得失，堪当大任。
commentaryEn: In this chapter, Laozi explains the meanings of “being dismayed by both favor and disgrace” and “valuing great misfortune as one values the body.” He also discusses what kind of person can be entrusted with the world. Laozi points to a weakness in human nature: people are deeply concerned with personal gain and loss. They are easily disturbed by both favor and disgrace, reacting to either as if it were a serious illness. Those in a subordinate position become uneasy when they receive favor from those above, and distressed when they lose it. This is what is meant by “being dismayed by both favor and disgrace.” Laozi further explains that our sense of misfortune arises from our attachment to the body, which is subject to illness and unforeseen harm. If one were without a body, there would be no cause for worry. Therefore, only those who value the world as they value their own body are fit to govern it, and only those who care for the world as they care for their own body are worthy of being entrusted with all under Heaven. Such a ruler truly follows the Tao. This chapter highlights the point of shattering the ego, relinquishing selfish desires, and serving the world selflessly. Only then can one transcend gain and loss and bear great trust.

title: 赞玄
original: 视之不见名曰夷。听之不闻名曰希。抟之不得名曰微。此三者不可致诘，故混而为一。其上不皦(jiǎo)，其下不昧，绳绳不可名，复归於无物。是谓无状之状，无物之象，是谓惚恍。迎之不见其首，随之不见其後。执古之道以御今之有。能知古始，是谓道纪。
translation: The fact that the Tao cannot be seen is called “Yi" (the invisible) because it has no color; The fact that the Tao cannot be heard is called “Xi" (the inaudible) because it has no sound; The fact that the Tao cannot be touched is called “Wei" (the intangible) because it has no shape. Because of these three characteristics, the Tao cannot be directly examined and defined and these three merge into One. Above it there is no brightness and below it there is no darkness. It fails to be described because it seems vague and vast; It reverts to the state of nothingness. That's why it is called "the Shapeless Shape" and "the Image of Nothingness"; That's why it is called "the Elusive". Looking up at it, you fail to see its head; Following behind it, you fail to see its tail. If you are able to lay hold of the ancient Tao, you will be able to guide and control the present. Comprehending the origin of the universe means you will be able to grasp the law of the Tao.
commentaryZh: 老子在本章中描述了“道”的几个特征（“夷”“希”“微”“惚恍”）以及掌握“道”的规律就可了解宇宙的规律等内容。“道”是看不见的、无色的，这个特征叫“夷”（yí）；“道”是听不见的、无声的，这个特征叫“希”（xī）；“道”是无形的、触摸不到的，这个特征叫“微”（wēi）。这三个特征很难区分开来，因此它们三者是浑然一体的。这个“一”就是“一阴一阳之谓道”的“一”，也就是“道”。“道”的这三个特征告诉我们，“道”是用心来悟的。这个“一”的上面不显得明亮，下面也不显得昏暗，它绵延无尽而又不可名状，最后又回到看不见的、虚无缥缈的状态。这种无形的形状，没有具体物质的形象，就是“道”的“惚恍”特征。抬头看不见它的头，跟在它后面又看不到它的尾。如果能掌握亘古就已经存在的“道”的运行规律，来探究我们现实中遇到的具体情况和事物，我们就能推知万事万物的运行规律，这就是“道”的规律。
commentaryEn: In this chapter, Laozi describes several qualities of the Tao and explains that understanding the Tao makes it possible to grasp the fundamental patterns of the universe. The Tao is invisible, which is called yi. It is inaudible, which is called xi. It is intangible, which is called wei. These three qualities cannot really be separated and together form a single unity. This unity is the “one” , which refers to the combination of yin and yang, which constitutes the Tao. Theses three qualities suggest that the Tao cannot be perceived through the senses but must be understood inwardly. It is neither bright above nor dark below, extending endlessly and defying any precise description before returning once again to an indistinct and elusive state. This formlessness is what Laozi calls the elusive quality of the Tao. One cannot see its beginning when looking ahead, nor its tail when following behind it. By grasping the enduring principles of the Tao, one can understand the patterns governing all things. This is what Laozi means by the law of the Tao.

title: 显德
original: 古之善为士者，微妙玄通，深不可识。夫唯不可识，故强为之容。豫兮若冬涉川；犹兮若畏四邻；俨兮其若容；涣兮若冰之将释；敦兮其若朴；旷兮其若谷；混兮其若浊；澹兮其若海；飉(liáo,风的声音)兮若无止。孰能浊以静之徐清。孰能安以动之徐生。保此道者不欲盈。夫唯不盈故能蔽而新成。
translation: Those ancient people well versed in the Tao were profound, subtle and mysterious; That's why people failed to understand them. However, the effort has to be made to describe how they behaved in daily life:They were cautious and hesitant as if crossing a river barefot in winter;They were vigilant and on guard as if fearing being attacked from all sides;They were dignified and formal as if they were guests; They were simple and natural as if ice began to thaw; They were unaffected and honest as if they were a piece of uncarved wood; They were open-minded and deep like a valley; They appeared muddled and foolish like muddy water. Who is able to end this muddy state? By staying still, the water gradually becomes clear. Who is able to maintain this calm state? By moving, things slowly come back to life.
commentaryZh: 本章是老子对古时有“道”之人的描述，也可以看作是老子对有“道”之人的画像。古时那些善于悟“道”、行“道”之人都是思想幽远、洞察力微妙深刻之人。因为他们深藏不露，世人无法了解他们幽深玄奥的思想，所以老子勉强用了几个比喻来描述他们：因谨慎小心而犹豫不决，如同在冬天涉水过河一样；警觉的样子，好像有敌人从四面八方来偷袭，保持四处张望的警惕状态；严肃拘谨的样子，仿佛是在别人家做客；处事心态坦然、顺天应人及柔和可亲的姿态，如正缓缓消融的冰一样坦荡悠然；淳朴厚道如未经雕琢的原木；心胸宽广豁达如空旷的山谷；浑厚宽容的态度使他混同于尘世，如浑浊的江水流淌。谁能在浑浊动荡中安静下来？静下来浑浊的水就会慢慢清净。谁能使安静的状态持久呢？变动起来的事物就会慢慢有生机。保持着这种“道”的人，是不会骄傲自满的。因为从不自满骄傲，不走极端，才能去旧更新。
commentaryEn: In this chapter, Laozi describes those in ancient times who followed the Tao, which may also be regarded as a portrait of such people. Those who were able to comprehend and practice the Tao in ancient times were individuals of profound thought and insight. Because they never showed themselves off, ordinary people could not fully understand them. Laozi therefore resorts to several metaphors to describe them. They moved with caution, like someone crossing a river in winter. They remained alert and watchful, as if aware of danger on every side. Their manner was reserved, like that of a guest in someone else’s home. At the same time, they were gentle and yielding, like ice gradually melting away. Their nature was plain and unadorned, like uncarved wood; their minds were open and receptive, like an empty valley. Broad and tolerant, they blended with the dust of the world like muddy water flowing in a river. Who can bring stillness to what is troubled? When left to settle, muddy water gradually becomes clear. Who can sustain quietude? From stillness, life slowly begins to stir. Those who live in accordance with the Tao therefore avoid arrogance and self-satisfaction. Because they never push things to extremes, they are able to renew themselves.

title: 归根
original: 致虚极守静笃。万物并作，吾以观复。夫物芸芸各复归其根。归根曰静，是谓复命；复命曰常，知常曰明。不知常，妄作凶。知常容，容乃公，公乃全，全乃天，天乃道，道乃久，没身不殆。
translation: A state of extreme emptiness and tranquility is needed to observe the recurrent cycles of the myriad things which flourish and die. In spite of their great variety, the myriad things eventually return to their respective roots. Returning to their respective roots is called "Tranquility", which is called "Returning to Destiny". Returning to destiny is called "Eternity"; Understanding this eternity is called "Enlightenment'". Those who fail to understand eternity and act rashly will eventually incur disasters. Understanding eternity enables one to be tolerant and all-encompassing, which enables one to be impartial, which enables one to be a qualified lord; He acts in accord with Heaven, and Heaven follows the Tao; The Tao is eternal; Therefore, whoever follows the Tao will stay away from danger and harm his whole life.
commentaryZh: 本章重点论述如何从纷纷纭纭、看似杂乱无章的万事万物背后洞察其运行的根本规律。老子用了一个极其关键的词：复。“复”就是反复、循环往复的意思，这是观察事物内在规律极其有效的根本途径。《易经》中第二十四卦就是“复卦”。想要达到以“复”观察万物之规律的状态，那就要使自己的心灵放空至极点，使生命的清净状态达到极致。在万物蓬勃成长的过程中，我观察到了它们生死循环、生生不息的规律。天下万物纷繁成长，但最终它们都将回归各自的根本。回归根本就是“静”，而静就是回归生命的本性。回归本性就是万事万物所遵循的不变的法则，即“道”的规律。能洞察这一点就是“明”，即“通明”。不能领悟这个法则并胡作非为就是凶险的，必定会招致灾祸。领悟到这个法则的人就会心胸宽广，就能包容与宽容，就不会有私心。宽容的人就会做事坦荡公平，而坦荡公平的人才有资格成为王者，王者会顺天道而为，顺天应“道”而运转，而“道”是永恒长久的。所以，顺“道”而为才会长生久视，终身远离危险与伤害。
commentaryEn: In this chapter, Laozi focuses on how one may discern the fundamental pattern underlying the seemingly chaotic and diverse phenomena of the world. To explain this idea, he employs a crucial concept: return. “Return” refers to repetition and cyclical movement, and it provides an effective way to perceive the inner order of things. In the Book of Changes, the twenty-fourth hexagram is called Return (Fu hexagram). To observe the laws of the myriad things through this principle of return, one must empty his mind and remain tranquil. As all things flourish and grow, Laozi observes the cycle of life and death through which they endlessly renew themselves. Although the myriad things in the world develop in countless ways, they ultimately return to their roots. Returning to the root means tranquility, and tranquility signifies a return to the original nature of life. Returning to this nature is the unchanging principle followed by all things—that is, the principle of the Tao. To perceive this principle is to be enlightened. Those who fail to understand it and act recklessly will inevitably encounter danger and misfortune. One who understands this principle becomes broad-minded and tolerant, free from selfish motives. Such a person acts with fairness and openness, and only those who possess such qualities are fit to become rulers. A true ruler acts in accordance with the way of Heaven and follows the Tao in governing the world. Since the Tao is eternal and enduring, those who act in accordance with it may enjoy longevity and remain free from danger and harm throughout their lives.

title: 淳风
original: 太上，下知有之。其次，亲而誉之。其次，畏之。其次，侮之。信不足焉，有不信焉。悠兮其贵言，功成事遂，百姓皆谓∶我自然。
translation: The best ruler is one whose existence is barely known to his people; The second best is one whom his people love and praise; The next comes the ruler feared by his people; The worst ruler is one who is cursed and disdained by his people. Such a ruler is not trustworthy, which explains the fact that he is distrusted by his people. The best ruler practices non-action, issuing fewer orders that harm the benefits of the people. Once things are done, the people all remark, "It should have happened to us naturally like this. "
commentaryZh: 老子在本章中把统治者划分成四个等级。最高级的统治者被称为“太上”，老百姓仅仅知道他的存在；第二级别的统治者是被百姓爱戴和赞美的；第三级别的统治者是百姓畏惧的；第四级别的统治者是最差的，因为是被百姓辱骂和要推翻的。统治者不讲信用，欺骗人民，自然就没有百姓信任他。最好的统治者谨慎而悠闲“无为”，不乱发号施令。有了功绩或事业完成，百姓都会理所当然地说：我们本来就这样啊！这种治理国家的方式就是君王顺应“道”而治，对百姓的生产和生活不过多干预，最终达到政府与人民和谐共处的双赢局面。
commentaryEn: In this chapter, Laozi classifies rulers into four levels. The best ruler is called the “supreme” one, whose existence the people are merely aware of. The second best is loved and praised by the people. The next is feared by them. The worst is despised by the people and even overthrown by them. When rulers are untrustworthy and deceive the people, it is natural that the people will no longer trust them. The best rulers govern with restraint, practicing non-action and refraining from issuing excessive commands. When achievements are made and tasks are accomplished, the people naturally say, “We have always been like this.” Such governance reflects a ruler who governs in accordance with the Tao. He interferes as little as possible with the people’s production and daily life, allowing government and people to coexist in harmony.

title: 俗薄
original: 大道废有仁义；慧智出有大伪；六亲不和有孝慈；国家昏乱有忠臣。
translation: With the decline of the great Tao, arose the necessity of advocating benevolence and justice; With the emergence of cunning knowledge and cleverness, appeared the great hypocrisy; With the deterioration of family relationships, such concepts as "filial piety"and "parental kindness" gained utmost importance; With great chaos prevailing in a country, loyal ministers were recognized.
commentaryZh: 老子在本章中指出：当大道被废弃了，也就是统治者没有施行“无为而治”，才有了提倡仁义的必要；当智谋、智巧出现了，虚伪狡诈也就随之出现了，欺骗就会盛行；当六亲（父子、兄弟、夫妻）不和出现了，就有了提倡孝慈的必要；当国家陷于混乱了，才能分出谁是忠臣。其实，老子在这一章要表达的是：如果大道盛行，其他的都是虚名与浮云。
commentaryEn: In this chapter, Laozi points out that only when the Great Tao is abandoned, that is, when rulers fail to govern through non-action, do benevolence and righteousness become necessary. When cleverness and cunning appear, hypocrisy and deceit follow and become widespread. When harmony within family relations (such as father and son, brothers, and husband and wife) breaks down, the promotion of filial piety and parental affection becomes necessary. Only when the state falls into disorder can loyal ministers be distinguished. What Laozi ultimately intends to convey in this chapter is that when the Great Tao prevails, all these virtues become mere empty names.

title: 还淳
original: 绝圣弃智，民利百倍；绝仁弃义，民复孝慈；绝巧弃利，盗贼无有；此三者，以为文不足。故令有所属，见素抱朴少私寡欲。
translation: If such concepts as cunning knowledge and cleverness are forsaken, the people will benefit from it a hundredfold; If such concepts as benevolence and righteousness are discarded, the people will become filial and kind spontaneously; If such concepts as artfulness and profit are rejected, theft and robbery will disappear. The above-mentioned three are merely decorations and not enough to be used for governing a state. Therefore, another ideological pattern is provided for the people to follow:Embrace simplicity and honesty, and diminish selfishness and desires; Forsake cunning knowledge and cleverness and worries will disappear.
commentaryZh: 本章可以看作是上一章的延续，强调摒弃“圣、仁、巧”等人为的巧饰与巧智，天下自然回归太平。（统治阶级）断绝和抛弃巧智与奸诈，百姓就会得到百倍的实惠；统治阶级摈弃仁爱与忠义的倡导，百姓就会回复到孝慈与家庭和睦的状态；舍弃骗人的技巧和追逐私利的行为，盗贼行为就会失去存在的土壤。用圣智、仁义、巧利粉饰社会和教化百姓是不足够的，因为它们只是表面形式，必须教化百姓遵循如下原则：见素抱朴（恪守纯真质朴的品性），少私寡欲（减少私利和欲望），绝学无忧（摈弃巧智就没有后顾之忧）。
commentaryEn: This chapter can be regarded as a continuation of the previous one. It emphasizes the need to abandon contrived qualities such as cunning knowledge, benevolence and artfulness, so that the world may naturally return to harmony and peace. If the ruler renounces cunning wisdom and deceit, the people will gain a hundredfold benefit. If rulers cease promoting benevolence and righteousness, the people will return to filial piety, parental affection, and harmony within the family. If deceptive skills and the pursuit of private profit are abandoned, theft and banditry will disappear. Laozi argues that relying on cunning wisdom, benevolence, righteousness, and clever profit to regulate society and instruct the people is insufficient, because these are merely outward forms. Instead, the people should be guided to follow more fundamental principles: embrace simplicity, reduce selfish desires, and abandon contrived knowledge, thereby becoming free from anxiety.

title: 异俗
original: 绝学无忧，唯之与阿，相去几何？善之与恶，相去若何？人之所畏，不可不畏。荒兮其未央哉！众人熙熙如享太牢、如春登台。我独泊兮其未兆，如婴儿之未孩；儡儡(lěi,羸弱)兮若无所归。众人皆有馀，而我独若遗。我愚人之心也哉！沌沌兮。俗人昭昭，我独昏昏；俗人察察，我独闷闷。众人皆有以，而我独顽且鄙。我独异於人，而贵食母。
translation: Is there any real diff erence between ' “yes”and “no"? Is there any real difference between "good" and “evil'"? I have to fear what others fear. The sea of such fear is, however, vast and boundless! The multitudes are merry-making as if enjoying a grand feast or mounting a tower to appreciate spring scenery . I alone remain peaceful and carefree like an infant who has not yet learned to smile; I appear weary like a homeless wanderer. I alone appear poor enough while others all have more than enough. I must be a muddleheaded man! The vulgar all look flamboyant and impressive while I alone appear dull andmuddleheaded. The vulgar all look brilliant and smart while I alone appear clumsy and unresponsive. My heart is patient like a vast and calm sea. I drift with wind, aimlessly but leisurely. The vulgar all look eager and purposeful while I alone appear stupid andunrefined. I alone differ from them in that I hold dear the Tao.
commentaryZh: 本章可以看作老子的自画像。老子以一个得道者的形象出现，他把自己与没有得道的人，即俗人进行了比较，生动地体现了一位得道者的精神风貌。老子认为恭敬的回答与略带虚情假意的应允的差别以及善恶的区别都是相对的，体现了他的辩证法思想。老子也明白大家都畏惧的事自己也要畏惧，一个人再强也得遵守公序良俗。老子觉得这种情况荒唐，但这种情况却持续了很久，而且还在继续。作为一位得道高人，老子用形象的比喻来突出俗人与得道之人的区别：俗人喜欢热热闹闹、吃喝玩乐、野心勃勃、追名逐利、富有潇洒、精明苛求，而得道之人看上去单纯无知、迷迷糊糊、淡泊恬静如广阔静谧的大海、无欲无求、浑浑噩噩、贫穷无居所如风中孤舟、愚钝顽鄙、单纯得如婴儿还未学会笑的样子。老子最后强调：因为自己以守“道”为贵，故与俗人有天壤之别。该章的主旨是老子极力主张返璞归真。老子提倡拒绝随波逐流、超越世俗评判、复归纯朴自然的天性。
commentaryEn: This chapter can be regarded as a self-portrait of Laozi. He presents himself as one who has attained the Tao and contrasts himself with ordinary people who have not. Through this comparison, Laozi vividly depicts the distinctive character of a person who follows the Tao. He suggests that the difference between a respectful and a perfunctory response, as well as the distinction between good and evil, is relative in nature, reflecting his dialectical mode of thinking. Laozi also acknowledges that what everyone fears should likewise be feared by him; no matter how capable a person may be, he must still observe the norms and conventions of society. Laozi finds this situation somewhat absurd, yet it has persisted for a long time and continues even now. As one who has attained the Tao, Laozi employs vivid metaphors to highlight the contrast between ordinary people and those who follow the Tao. Ordinary people delight in excitement, indulgence, ambition, and the pursuit of fame and profit; they appear prosperous and calculating. By contrast, those who follow the Tao seem simple and even somewhat ignorant, indistinct and detached, calm and tranquil like the vast and quiet sea. They are free from desire and unconcerned with worldly gains. They may appear dull and clumsy, poor and without a fixed dwelling, like a solitary boat drifting in the wind. Yet they remain pure and simple, like an infant who has not yet learned to smile. Laozi concludes by emphasizing that because he values and preserves the Tao, he stands in sharp contrast to ordinary people. The core theme of this chapter is returning to original purity. He advocates refusing to follow the crowd, transcending worldly judgments, and restoring one’s pure, natural and innate nature.

title: 虚心
original: 孔德之容惟道是从。道之为物惟恍惟惚。惚兮恍兮其中有象。恍兮惚兮其中有物。窈兮冥兮其中有精。其精甚真。其中有信。自古及今，其名不去以阅众甫。吾何以知众甫之状哉！以此。
translation: Great virtue takes the Tao as its sole criterion. The Tao is something difficult to define in that it is elusive and vague. Yet in its elusiveness and vagueness there seem to be images; In its vagueness and elusiveness there seem to be materials. It is far and dim, yet there is some essence. This essence is something genuine, which can be tested as true. From earliest times to now, the Tao has been in existence; By observing the Tao I survey how all things came into being. How do I know about the beginning of the myriad things? I know about it based on the Tao.
commentaryZh: 本章重点描述了“道”的“恍惚”特征。大德所遵循的唯一标准就是“道”。 “道”这种东西其表现状态是恍恍惚惚，即模糊不清、无形无状。在惚惚恍恍中有“道”的形象，而在恍恍惚惚中有“道”的实物。“道”是那么幽远昏暗，其中可以感受到它的精气。这种精气极其真实，而这种真实是可信的、可以验证的。从古至今，它的名字从未消失，人们可以通过观察它认识万物的起源。我是如何了解到万物的起始情况的呢？是根据“道”认识的。
commentaryEn: In this chapter, Laozi mainly describes the “vague and elusive” nature of the Tao. For those who possess great virtue, the Tao is the only standard they follow. The Tao appears in an elusive and vague state—obscure, formless, and difficult to grasp. Within this elusiveness and vagueness, there seem to be images, and within this vagueness and elusiveness there appear to be things. The Tao is deep and mysterious, yet within it one can perceive its vital essence. This essence is exceedingly real, and this reality is trustworthy and verifiable. From ancient times until now, its name has never vanished, and through it people can come to understand the origin of all things. How do I know the beginnings of the myriad things? It is through the Tao.

title: 益谦
original: 曲则全，枉则直，洼则盈，敝则新少则得，多则惑。是以圣人抱一为天下式。不自见故明；不自是故彰；不自伐故有功；不自矜故长；夫唯不争，故天下莫能与之争。古之所谓∶曲则全者」岂虚言哉！诚全而归之。
translation: To stoop is to stay whole; To bend is to become straight; To lie low is to be filled up; Only the old can be renewed; To seek little is to gain much; Being greedy brings confusion. Therefore: The sage embraces One (the Tao), regarding it as the model for the world. He does not display himsel, and fr that he becomes more enlightened; He does not justify himself, and for that he is more apt to distinguish right from wrong; He does not boast about his achievements, and for that he becomes more well- known; He does not pride himself on his merits, and for that his fame endures longer. He does not contend, and for that no one can contend with him. As the ancients put it, "To stoop is to stay whole." Are these empty words? They can be proven effective indeed.
commentaryZh: 老子在本章中重点论述了他的“曲则全”的哲学思想的内涵并举例进一步阐释了这一思想。老子说委屈反而能保全自己，弯曲才能伸直，处于低洼才能得到充盈，破旧反而容易更新，少欲反而多得，贪多反而会心意迷乱。因此，有道的圣人坚守“一”的原则，即将“道”的原则作为治理天下的范式。不炫耀自己反而会彰显自己；不自以为是，不总是主观上认为自己一定是对的，反而是非清晰；不自我表扬、吹嘘反而功绩自然就来了；不骄傲狂妄反而能成长、长久。由于谦虚不争，所以天下人没有谁能够与他争高低。古人所说的“曲则全”这句话所蕴含的道理可不是空话啊！那是完完全全可以达到的。
commentaryEn: In this chapter, Laozi elaborates on the philosophical idea of “To stoop is to stay whole” and further illustrates this principle through a series of examples. Laozi states that yielding can preserve oneself, bending allows one to become straight, dwelling in low places enables one to be filled, and what is worn out can more easily be renewed. Having few desires brings abundance, whereas excessive desires lead to confusion of the mind. Therefore, the sage who follows the Tao upholds the principle of the One---the Tao, taking it as the model for his governance. One who does not display himself will become distinguished; one who is not self-righteous can clearly discern right from wrong; one who does not boast of his achievements naturally gains merit; and one who is not arrogant can endure and develop. Because he is humble and does not contend, no one in the world can compete with him. The ancient saying “To stoop is to stay whole” is therefore far from empty rhetoric. It expresses a principle that can indeed be realized.

title: 虚无
original: 希言自然。故飘风不终朝，骤雨不终日。孰为此者？天地。天地尚不能久，而况於人乎？故从事於道者，同於道。德者同於德。失者同於失。同於道者道亦乐得之；同於德者德亦乐得之；同於失者失於乐得之信不足焉有不信焉。
translation: If possible, a ruler should issue fewer orders, which is in accord with Nature (the Tao) . This can be perceived through such natural phenomena: A wind storm does not last a whole morning and a rainstorm does not outlast a whole day. Who causes these? Heaven and Earth. If what Heaven and Earth make cannot last long, how can a ruler's tyranny? Therefore: He who follows the Tao acts in accord with the Tao; He who follows virtue acts in accord with virtue; He who goes against the Tao and virtue will be abandoned by them. The Tao is glad to welcome him who acts in accord with it; Virtue is glad to welcome him who acts in accord with it; Whoever abandons the Tao will be abandoned by it; Whoever abandons virtue will be abandoned by it. Whoever lacks trustworthiness will be distrusted by others.
commentaryZh: 在本章中，老子认为统治者应该克制欲望，少发号施令干预民生，这样做才符合自然规律，也就是符合“道”的规律。老子进一步比喻说：再大的狂风也刮不过一个早晨，再大的暴雨也不会持续一天。谁制造了狂风暴雨呢？是天地。就连天地制造的风雨现象都不能持久，何况国君治国时频繁颁布的那些干涉万物、背离“道”的法令呢？所以当修道者的行为符合“道”的规律时，他的行为就融入了“道”；修德的人的行为符合“德”的标准时，他的行为就融入了“德”；妄作胡为的人，他的行为就是背离“道”与“德”，这种人必将暴力施虐，下场可悲。凡是尊“道”贵“德”之人，“道”与“德”也乐于得到他；而失“道”失“德”的人，也将会被“道”与“德”抛弃。统治者寡信，老百姓自然就不会信任他。
commentaryEn: In this chapter, Laozi argues that rulers should restrain their desires and refrain from issuing excessive commands that interfere with the livelihood of the people. Only in this way can governance accord with the natural order, that is, with the Tao. Laozi further illustrates this idea metaphorically: even the strongest wind cannot last through the entire morning, and even the heaviest rain cannot continue for an entire day. Who produces these violent winds and storms? Heaven and Earth. Yet even the phenomena created by Heaven and Earth cannot endure for long, how could the numerous decrees issued by rulers possibly endure? Therefore, when the conduct of those who cultivate the Tao accords with it, their actions become one with it. When the conduct of those who cultivate virtue conforms to virtue, their actions become united with virtue. Those who act recklessly, however, deviate from both the Tao and virtue, and such people will inevitably resort to violence and meet a tragic end. Those who honor the Tao and virtue are in turn embraced by them, whereas those who lose the Tao and virtue will likewise be abandoned by them. When rulers lack credibility, the people will naturally cease to trust them.

title: 苦恩
original: 企者不立；跨者不行。自见者不明；自是者不彰。自伐者无功；自矜者不长。其在道也曰∶馀食赘形。物或恶之，故有道者不处。
translation: He who stands on tiptoe to gain stature fails to stand steady; He who doubles his strides to go ahead fails to walk faster; He who displays himself fails to perceive the truth; He who justifies himself fails to distinguish right from wrong; He who boasts about his achievements fails to become more well-known; He who prides himself on his merits fails to keep his fame longer. From the perspective of the Tao, the above-mentioned behavior is like nothing but leftover food and proud flesh despised by people; Therefore, the man who follows the Tao stays away from these things of disgust.
commentaryZh: 老子在本章中重点论述了人性中“急功近利”和“急躁炫耀”的行为，这些行为（企、跨、自见、自是、自伐、自矜）如残渣剩饭、人身上的赘肉，令人厌烦、憎恶。老子说踮起脚尖站立，是站不牢的，也站不久；两步并作一步地走，是走不了太远的，是脚步跨得太大的缘故；一个人炫耀自己反而不会彰显自己；自以为是，总是主观上认为自己一定是对的，就无法分清是非；自我表扬、自我吹嘘反而得不到功绩；骄傲狂妄的人无法成长、长久。因为这些行为都是违背“道”的规律的，有道之人绝不会这样做。本章“自见者不明；自是者不彰；自伐者无功；自矜者不长”与二十二章“不自见，故明；不自是，故彰；不自伐，故有功；不自矜，故长”的论述正是老子正反论述的语言特征的案例。
commentaryEn: In this chapter, Laozi criticizes quick success and restless self-display, which are weaknesses in human nature. Behaviors such as standing on tiptoe, striding too far, self-assertion, self-righteousness, self-praise, and self-conceit are compared to leftovers and tumors on the body, which are unpleasant and detestable. Laozi explains that one who stands on tiptoe cannot stand firmly for long. One who tries to take strides that are too large cannot go very far. A person who shows himself off will not truly become distinguished. One who believes himself always right cannot clearly distinguish right from wrong. Those who boast of themselves gain no real merit, and those who are arrogant and self-conceited cannot endure or develop. These behaviors are doomed to failure because they run counter to the Tao. A person who follows the Tao would never act in such ways. The statements in this chapter—“He who displays himself fails to perceive the truth; he who justifies himself fails to distinguish right from wrong; he who boasts about his achievements fails to become more well-known; he who prides himself on his merits fails to keep his fame longer” form a clear contrast with Chapter 22, which expresses the same idea in the opposite way. This contrast exemplifies Laozi’s rhetorical pattern of presenting ideas through both positive and negative formulations.

title: 象元
original: 有物混成先天地生。寂兮寥兮独立不改，周行而不殆，可以为天下母。吾不知其名，强字之曰道。强为之名曰大。大曰逝，逝曰远，远曰反。故道大、天大、地大、人亦大。域中有大，而人居其一焉。人法地，地法天，天法道，道法自然。
translation: There was something chaotic before the birth of Heaven and Earth. Silent, vast and formless, it stands alone and changeless, eternally moving in circle endlessly; It can be called the Mother of Heaven and Earth. I have no idea about its name; If compelled to name it, I would like to call it “Tao" ; If compelled to describe it, I would like to call it "Great" . Being great means flowing away in space; Flowing away in space means reaching far; Reaching far means returning to the original point. Therefore: The Tao is great; Heaven is great; Earth is great; Man is great as well. There are four great things in the universe, and man is one of them. Man patterns himself on Earth; Earth patterns itself on Heaven; Heaven patterns itself on the Tao; The Tao is its being what it is.
commentaryZh: 本章是《道德经》中最重要的章节之一，与第一章遥相呼应，提出“道”是宇宙生命的本体与本源。老子说“有物混成，先天地生”，他论述了“道”的“物质性”及“先天性”，凸显了他的唯物主义思想。这种“浑然而成”的“道”寂静无声而又广阔无形，它独立存在而又永不枯竭，周而复始地运行而又永不停息，这个“道”可以被认为是宇宙万物的根源。我不知道它的名字，勉强称呼它为“道”，勉强形容它为“大”。“大”的意思是“道”无边无垠而运行不息，运行不息而向远方无限延伸，而伸向幽远后又返回原点或本真。“道”无处不在，所以“大”，天也同样“大”，地也同样“大”，人也同样“大”。宇宙间有这“四大”，而人也在其列。这也是老子人文主义思想的体现。所以，人要效法地，地要效法天，天要效法“道”，而“道”本来就是那个样子。在最后这句话中，老子运用了“搭梯子”的顶真格句式，突出这句话的主语是“人”，即：人法地、人法天、人法道。
commentaryEn: This is one of the most important chapters in Tao Te Ching. It echoes the first chapter and proposes that the Tao is the ontological foundation and ultimate source of life in the universe. Laozi states that “there was something chaotic born before Heaven and Earth”. He discusses both the material character and the primordial nature of the Tao, highlighting the materialist tendency in his thought. This Tao, which arises naturally, is silent and tranquil, yet vast and formless. It exists independently and never becomes exhausted. It operates in cyclical motion without ever ceasing. This Tao may be regarded as the origin of all things in the universe. Laozi says, “I do not know its name, so I reluctantly call it ‘Tao’, and I reluctantly describe it as ‘great.’” The meaning of “great” is that the Tao is boundless and constantly in motion. In its ceaseless movement it extends endlessly into the distance, and after reaching the farthest point it returns to its origin or authentic state. Because the Tao is everywhere, it is therefore great. Heaven is likewise great, Earth is likewise great, and humanity is likewise great. In the universe there are these four great things, and human beings are among them. This also reflects the humanistic dimension of Laozi’s thought. Therefore, human beings follow the model of Earth, Earth follows the model of Heaven, Heaven follows the Tao, and the Tao follows what is natural to itself. In the final sentence, Laozi uses a chain-like structure to highlight the subject: humans follow Earth, follows the heaven and finally the Tao.

title: 重德
original: 重为轻根，静为躁君。是以君子终日行不离轻重。虽有荣观燕处超然。奈何万乘之主而以身轻天下。轻则失根，躁则失君。
translation: Weightiness is the root of lightness; Quietude is the master of frenzy. Therefore the sage travels all day, yet never strays away from his baggage wagon.In spite of basking in honor and glory, he resides tranquilly without being distracted by his luxurious surroundings. Why does a ruler of a great country take his governance so lightly? Lightness leads to the loss of the root; Frenzy results in the loss of rationality.
commentaryZh: 在本章中，老子重点论述了如何克服人性的弱点——轻浮和躁动。稳重与庄重是克服轻浮的根本，安静和清净是制服躁动的主宰。所以，有道的君王终日依“道”行事，就像行军打仗一样时刻不离辎重，因为辎重是打胜仗的根本保障之一。有道的君王即使有机会享受荣华富贵，他们也能超然物外，淡然处之， 绝不沉迷其中而不能自拔。为何大国君王在治理国家的时候还会轻率鲁莽行事呢？轻率、轻浮就会失去根本，就会失控，就会失败；急躁、浮躁就会失去理性的主宰和控制，必然走向灭亡。
commentaryEn: In this chapter, Laozi focuses on how to overcome two weaknesses of human nature—frivolity and restlessness. Composure and seriousness are the fundamental means of overcoming frivolity, while tranquility and inner calm are the key to restraining restlessness. Therefore, a ruler who follows the Tao acts in accordance with it throughout the day, just as an army on campaign never parts from its baggage train, for such supplies are an essential guarantees of victory. Even when rulers who follow the Tao have the opportunity to enjoy wealth and luxury, they remain detached and treat them with indifference, never becoming so absorbed in them that they lose themselves. Why, then, do other rulers still act rashly and recklessly in governing their countries? Acting lightly and frivolously leads to the loss of one’s foundation, to loss of control, and ultimately to failure. Impatience and frivolity cause one to lose rational judgment and self-restraint, and will inevitably lead to ruin.

title: 巧用
original: 善行无辙迹。善言无瑕谪。善数不用筹策。善闭无关楗而不可开。善结无绳约而不可解。是以圣人常善救人，故无弃人。常善救物，故无弃物。是谓袭明。故善人者不善人之师。不善人者善人之资。不贵其师、不爱其资，虽智大迷，是谓要妙。
translation: One who is good at walking leaves no traces; One who is good at speaking leaves no flaws for ridicule; One who is good at counting needs no counting tools; One who is good at locking up needs no bolts, yet the door cannot be opened;One who is good at tying up needs no ropes, yet the knots cannot be untied. Therefore: The sage is good at saving people and for that no one is useless; He is good at making the most out of things, and for that nothing is wasted. This is profound wisdom. Therefore: A man who follows the Tao is the teacher of the man who goes against the Tao;A man who goes against the Tao serves as the negative teaching materials for the man who follows the Tao. One who neither cherishes his teacher nor takes others as the negative teaching materials is a big fool, though he may be bright and learned. This is subtle wisdom.
commentaryZh: 本章核心思想讲有道之人做事是“自然无为”，而非“强为”，如果做事处处留痕迹就背离了“道”的宗旨，是有功利心的表现。“善”字在这一章反复使用。老子连续用了“五善”来递进论述有道的人做事的境界。善于行走的人不会留下踪迹；善于讲话的人不会出现语言上的瑕疵；善于计数的人不用计算的工具；善于关门以防盗窃的人不用门闩别人也无法打开；善于用绳索捆缚的人不用绳结他人也无法解开。所以，有道的圣人善于挽救人，从不遗弃任何人。哪怕在常人看来毫无用处之人，他也善于做到物尽其用。在他眼里没有无用之物，万物皆可用。正如常言道：“看人所短，天下无可交之人；看人之长，世间一切尽是吾师。”这是深藏不露的智慧啊。因此，善人（有道的人）可以成为不善人的老师，而不善人可以成为善人学习的借鉴和参照物。一个人不尊重善人的教诲，不珍惜不善人的反面教材的借鉴作用，那么这个人即使聪明绝顶，其实也是个大糊涂！这里蕴含精深微妙的智慧啊！
commentaryEn: The central idea of this chapter is that those who follow the Tao act through non-action, rather than through forced action. When one’s actions deliberately leave visible traces, they deviate from the principle of the Tao and reveal a utilitarian mindset. In this chapter, Laozi uses instances of “goodness” to progressively illustrate the realm of those who follow the Tao. One who is good at walking leaves no tracks; one who is good at speaking makes no verbal errors; one who is good at counting needs no calculating tools; one who is good at closing a door requires no bolt, yet others cannot open it; and one who is good at binding with ropes needs no knots, yet others cannot untie it. Therefore, the sage who follows the Tao is good at saving people and never abandons anyone. Even those who are regarded as useless can be put to good use in his view. Likewise, nothing is truly useless; everything in the world has its value. As a common saying goes, “If one looks only at others’ shortcomings, there will be no one in the world worth associating with; if one looks at others’ strengths, everyone in the world can be one’s teacher in some respect.” This is wisdom that remains deeply concealed. Thus, the good person who follows the Tao can be a teacher to those who are not good, while those who are not good can serve as examples and points of reference from which the good may learn. If a person neither respects the guidance of the good nor values the instructive examples provided by those who are not good, then even if that person appears extremely intelligent, he is in fact profoundly mistaken. This truly is subtle and profound wisdom.

title: 反朴
original: 知其雄，守其雌，为天下溪。为天下溪，常德不离，复归於婴儿。知其白，守其黑，为天下式。为天下式，常德不忒，复归於无极。知其荣，守其辱，为天下谷。为天下谷，常德乃足，复归於朴。朴散则为器，圣人用之则为官长。故大制不割。
translation: He who knows the strength of masculinity but chooses to play the role of female is qualified to be the confluence of the world with al the tributaries flowing to him.Being the confluence of the world, he enjoys the eternal company of constant virtue; W ith the eternal company of constant virtue he returns to innocent infancy. He who knows the limelight but chooses to play the role of black is qualified to be a role model for the world. Being a role model for the world, he can be no longer at odds with constant virtue; Being no longer at odds with constant virtue, he returns to a state of boundlessness. He who knows glory but chooses to play the role of the disgraced is qualified to be the valley of the world. Being the valley of the world, he enjoys sufficient constant virtue; W ith sufficient constant virtue, he returns to a state of simplicity; When the simple Tao functions, the myriad things are created. With the Tao as his guide, a sage can be the ruler of a country. Therefore: The perfect government operates in accord with the Tao with no view to issuing orders that will harm the interests of the people.
commentaryZh: 本章是《道德经》中非常重要的一章，主要论述“常德”的“三知三守”。老子在这一章中运用了顶真格修辞手法来突出其核心思想。“雄与雌”“荣与辱”“白与黑”都是事物对立统一的“阴阳”两个方面，相互依赖。本章体现了老子的守柔哲学及其返璞归真才符合“道”的思想，也折射了老子“雌雄同体”（androgyny）的哲学理念。老子认为，只有明白了自己的雄强或自己拥有的核心竞争力，才能守住自己的雌或自己的柔弱并甘愿做天下溪水汇入的溪谷。甘愿做溪谷就会常德（永恒存在的自然之德）不离，即“道”的不流失、不离开，而回归到婴儿般纯真柔和的状态及无私无欲的境界。深知何为明亮、荣显，但安守暗昧或谦下，甘愿成为天下效仿的榜样。这样，常德就不会出差错并回归到不可穷极或无限可能的状态。深知荣耀辉煌的光鲜亮丽，但安守卑下和屈辱，甘愿做天下的川谷,保持空旷、虚空、无物不容的心态。这样，常德就永远丰足，而回归到质朴纯真的状态，即“朴”的状态，而“朴”即“道”。“朴”分散化育宇宙万物，就有了具体的器物，有道的人依“道”而行就会成为百官之长并建立管理天下的政治体制。所以，依据“道”而运行完善的政治制度如同完整不可分割的“道”一样，不能人为割裂、肢解。
commentaryEn: This chapter is a pivotal one in Tao Te Ching, focusing on the “Three Forms of Knowing and Three Forms of Preserving” associated with constant virtue (chang de). In this chapter, Laozi employs a chain-linked rhetorical structure to highlight his central ideas. Pairs such as strength and softness, honor and disgrace, and brightness and darkness represent the two complementary aspects of yin and yang, which exist in mutual dependence. The chapter reflects Laozi’s philosophy of preserving softness and his teaching that only by returning to simplicity and naturalness can one remain aligned with the Tao. It also reveals Laozi’s philosophical notion of androgyny, the integration of both the masculine and the feminine within a single unity. Laozi maintains that only by recognizing one’s own strengths can one preserve one’s softness and willingly become like a valley into which all streams flow. By accepting the role of the valley, constant virtue will not depart, meaning that the Tao will neither be lost nor abandoned, and one will return to a state of childlike purity and gentleness, free from selfish desire. One who clearly understands what is bright and honorable, yet remains content to dwell in obscurity and humility, willingly becomes a model for the world. In this way, constant virtue remains free from deviation and returns to a state of boundless possibility. One who deeply understands glory and splendor, yet abides in lowliness and even disgrace, willingly becomes like the great valleys of the world, maintaining a disposition that is open, empty, and receptive to all things. In this way, constant virtue remains ever abundant and returns to a state of simplicity, which is identical with the Tao. When this state of simplicity disperses and gives rise to the myriad things of the universe, concrete forms and instruments come into being. Those who follow the Tao in governing become leaders among officials and establish a political order for managing the world. Therefore, a political system that operates in accordance with the Tao should be whole and indivisible, just like the Tao itself, and must not be artificially fragmented or dismantled.

title: 无为
original: 将欲取天下而为之，吾见其不得已。天下神器，不可为也，为者败之，执者失之。夫物或行或随、或觑或吹、或强或羸、或挫或隳。是以圣人去甚、去奢、去泰。
translation: As for those who attempt to govern the country by force, I don't think they can make it. Governing the country successfully is a holy thing, which cannot be done by means of force. Those who attempt to govern the country through force are doomed to failure; Those who try to dominate the country through force will lose it sooner or later. People under Heaven are of different kinds in terms of temperament: Some are active while others are passive; some are warm-hearted while others are indifferent; some are strong while others are weak; some are reliable while others are dangerous . Therefore: The sage governs the country in accord with the Tao, paying enough heed to human nature and specific circumstances, which entails his practicing non-action and eliminating all radical measures in his governance.
commentaryZh: 在本章中，老子旗帜鲜明地提出了统治和管理国家最好的策略就是“无为”，因为“无为”是遵循天道而行。如果反其道而行之，靠武力、暴力、强权和暴政来夺取天下的君王必将下场凄惨。“天下神器”就是治理天下百姓的公权，也是神圣不可侵犯的江山社稷，这种权力绝不能公权私用或以君王个人意志为转移而滥用，这种权力的实施必须遵循“道”的原则，即“利而不害”，而要达到这个目标，就得严格遵守“无为而治”的政治理念。试图利用强力来获得“天下神器” 必将失败。圣人谙悉“道”的规律，以“无为”取天下，所以不会失败。天下之人的性情千差万别：有的主动，有的被动；有的温和，有的冷漠；有的强大，有的弱小；有的稳重，有的危险。所以，有道之人要顺应“天道”，治理天下要顺应民意 而非违背民意肆意妄为。这就需要圣人在治理天下的过程中，除掉极端的、奢侈的和过度的苛政措施，以顺应“天道”。
commentaryEn: In this chapter, Laozi explicitly proposes that the best strategy for ruling and governing a state is non-action, because non-action means acting in accordance with the Tao of Heaven. On the contrary, if rulers rely on force and tyranny to seize power, they will inevitably meet a tragic end. Governing the people and the state is a sacred matter, and therefore must not be exercised according to the ruler’s personal will. Instead, its exercise must follow the principles of the Tao, namely benefiting others without causing harm. To achieve this goal, a ruler must practice non-action. Any attempt to obtain such authority through force is bound to fail. By contrast, the sage who understands the Tao gains the world through non-action and therefore never fails. People in the world differ greatly in their dispositions: some are active while others are passive; some are gentle while others are indifferent; some are strong while others are weak; some are steady while others are reckless. Therefore, those who follow the Tao must conform to the Tao of Heaven. In governing the world, they should follow the will of the people rather than act arbitrarily against it. This requires rulers to eliminate extreme, extravagant, and excessively harsh policies in order to accord with the Tao of Heaven.

title: 俭武
original: 以道佐人主者，不以兵强天下。其事好还。师之所处荆棘生焉。军之後必有凶年。善有果而已，不敢以取强。果而勿矜。果而勿伐。果而勿骄。果而不得已。果而勿强。物壮则老，是谓不道，不道早已。
translation: He who assists the ruler of a country by virtue of the Tao will oppose the act of conquering other countries through military force for such conquest will lead to being conquered by the conquered in the long run: Wherever armies are, thorns and brambles spring up.After a bitter battle, a year of famine is sure to follow. Therefore: A good commander-in-chief will stop in due time after he has achieved his goal; He dares not to further display military strength.He does not claim credit for having achieved the goal;He does not boast about his success; He does not take pride in his achievements; He knows well that military actions are unavoidable and that there is no need for further action any more after achieving the purpose. Being in prime goes against the Tao; He who uses force and strength does not act in accord with the Tao; Whatever violates the Tao will come to an end soon.
commentaryZh:
本章体现了老子反战的和平思想。在老子看来，战争是与“道”相违背的行径。有道的人在辅佐君王治理天下时不会轻易发动战争，不因军事强大以武力征服天下，因为穷兵黩武会带来灾难性的后果，如劳动力奇缺、土地荒芜、哀鸿遍野、瘟疫横行、饥荒肆虐。善于用兵的人都是有道的人，当他们达到战争的目的后就会及时停止，不会以兵强马壮来耀武扬威，继续挑战而进一步扩大战争的范围。他们达到了目的也不会自大狂妄、自吹自擂、骄傲轻狂。即使达到目的，他们也深知战争是不得已而为之，深知逞强好胜必将走向覆灭。事物强大到极点就会向其反面发展，因为这种现象违背“道”的规律，不遵守“道”的行为必将很快走向衰败。
31 (到此）
本章是继上一章老子反战思想的延续。老子认为兵器是凶险的东西，为人所厌恶，有道的君王绝不会利用战争来解决问题。有道的君子平时居住以左边为尊贵，而在战争期间则以右为尊贵。这说明君王对战争性质的极度重视。兵器是灾难的象征，是有道君王所讨厌的东西，在别无选择或迫不得已的情况下才会选择使用（即：和平或不战而屈人之兵才是最好的途径），所以有道的君王在这个极其严肃的问题上最好慎之又慎。即使打了大胜仗也不要得意扬扬或赞美它。赞美胜利或因胜利而自以为了不起的人就是把杀人当成乐事的人。这种人绝不可能成为天下之主，因为他们嗜好杀戮，缺乏慈悲之心。人们在庆祝吉事的时候以左方为尊位，办丧事的时候以右方为尊位。行军打仗，兵权小的偏将军在左边，而兵权大的上将军在右边。这说明用兵打仗要严格以丧礼的仪式来处理涉及打仗的各项事宜。打仗会死很多人，要以悲哀的同理心对待死者。战胜了对方，也要以丧礼的仪式来对待或安葬死去的人。
commentaryEn: This chapter reflects Laozi’s anti-war thought. In Laozi’s view, war is an action that goes against the Tao. Those who follow the Tao, when assisting rulers in governance, do not lightly resort to warfare, nor do they rely on military strength to conquer the world by force. The reckless use of military power inevitably brings disastrous consequences, such as a severe shortage of labor, abandoned farmland, widespread suffering among the people, epidemics, and devastating famine. Those who are truly skilled in the use of military force are people who follow the Tao. Once they have achieved their objective, they stop immediately and do not display their military power or continue to expand the war. Even after achieving their aims, they do not boast about it or take pride in it. They understand that war is undertaken only as a last resort and that aggressive competitiveness will ultimately lead to destruction. When things reach their extreme, they inevitably turn toward their opposite. Such extremity violates the principle of the Tao, and any behavior that fails to accord with the Tao will quickly move toward decline. This chapter continues the anti-war ideas expressed in the previous chapter. Laozi believes that Weapons are ominous and dangerous objects that people naturally detest. A ruler who follows the Tao would never resort to war to resolve problems. A noble person who follows the Tao normally regards the left side as the place of honor, but during times of war the right side becomes the honored position. This reflects the ruler’s profound awareness of the grave nature of warfare. Weapons symbolize calamity and are detested by rulers who follow the Tao. They should be used only when there is no other choice. In other words, maintaining peace or subduing others without fighting is always the best choice. For this reason, a ruler who follows the Tao must treat the matter of war with the utmost caution. Even when a great victory is achieved, one should not take pride in it or praise it. To delight in victory or to praise it is to take pleasure in killing. Those who delight in killing can never become true rulers of the world, for they lack compassion and enjoy slaughter. In traditional ritual practice, the left side is honored during auspicious ceremonies, whereas the right side is honored during mourning rites. In military formations, a deputy general stands on the left, while the commanding general stands on the right. This arrangement indicates that matters of warfare should be treated in the same way as a mourning ceremony. Wars inevitably lead to the death of many people, who should be treated with equal empathy. Even victors should regard the dead with sorrow and sympathy and bury them according to mourning rites.

title: 偃武
original: 夫佳兵者不祥之器，物或恶之，故有道者不处。君子居则贵左，用兵则贵右。兵者不祥之器，非君子之器，不得已而用之，恬淡为上。胜而不美，而美之者，是乐杀人。夫乐杀人者，则不可得志於天下矣。吉事尚左，凶事尚右。偏将军居左，上将军居右。言以丧礼处之。杀人之众，以悲哀泣之，战胜以丧礼处之。
translation: Weapons are tools of calamity detested by all people; Therefore: The man who follows the Tao chooses not to use them. Such a man often values the auspicious left in daily life; Yet, in times of war, he positions himself on the inauspicious right. When war cannot be avoided, he should resort to military force with much restraint. When the victory is won, he should not delight in glorifying it; If he cannot help glorifying the victory, he must be a blood-thirsty man who takes delight in killing. Such a man is in no way qualified to govern the country. Auspicious occasions honor the left while inauspicious ones favor the right. Therefore: In times of war, the lieutenant general is seated on the left while the general is seated on the right. That is to say, war is a matter that should be treated as funeral affairs. A large number of people are killed in battles and the dead should be treated properly by the victor who closely observes mourning ceremonies; Thus, any victory should be treated solemnly in accord to funeral ceremonies.

title: 圣德
original: 道常无名。朴虽小天下莫能臣也。侯王若能守之，万物将自宾。天地相合以降甘露，民莫之令而自均。始制有名，名亦既有，夫亦将知止，知止可以不殆。譬道之在天下，犹川谷之於江海。
translation: The Tao is eternally nameless. It seems small, yet nothing under Heaven can dominate it. If rulers can stick to the Tao, the whole world will subject itself to them. When the Yin and the Yang between Heaven and Earth interact, sweet rain falls gently upon the myriad things on the earth, evenly distributed without any human interference. The Tao created all things and they were given names respectively; Names given, people should know well how to follow the Tao. Once a ruler knows when to stop, he will stay away from danger. The Tao prevailing under Heaven can be compared to the sea into which all rivers eventually flow.
commentaryZh: 本章讲述了“道”的另一个称呼“朴”及其作用。“道”永远没有名字，老子勉强把它称为“道”。老子也用“朴”来描述“道”的原始的质朴状态，它虽然细小到无法分辨，但天下没有谁能把它降服。相反，尊它守它的统治者如果能用它来治理国家，那么天下百姓都会愿意归顺于他。天地间阴阳两气交互，普降甘露滋润大地万物，甘露不需要任何人的指令，就会均匀分配，不偏不倚。这都是“道”的作用，而非人为之力。“道”化育万物，万物被确定了各自的名称，圣人治理天下开始建立制度法规，就有了各种法规名称和社会等级秩序。统治者要明白自己所处的位置及相应的制约，要适可而止。守好自己的本位，就不会有危险。大道无处不在，如同江海。统治者若能尊道而行“无为”之治，天下的百姓就会像天下的河流小溪主动流归江海一样，心甘情愿臣服于他。
commentaryEn: This chapter introduces another name for the Tao, “the small”, and its function. The Tao has no eternal name and Laozi only reluctantly calls it the Tao. He also uses the small to describe the Tao’s originality and simplicity. Although it is so subtle that it cannot be clearly distinguished, nothing in the world can subdue it. On the contrary, if rulers use it to govern the state, the people of the world will willingly submit to them. In heaven and earth, the two vital forces of yin and yang interact and bring down sweet dew that nourishes all things. This dew requires no command from anyone, yet it is distributed evenly and without partiality. All of this is the work of the Tao rather than human effort. The Tao generates and nurtures the myriad things, and once things come into being, they are given names. When sages govern the world, they begin to establish institutions and regulations, which in turn produce various rules, titles, and social hierarchies. Rulers must therefore understand their own position and the limits that accompany it, and they should know when to stop. By keeping to their proper place, they will avoid danger. The Great Tao is present everywhere, like rivers and seas. If rulers practice the Tao and govern through non-action, the people of the world will naturally submit to them, just as the streams and rivers of the world flow willingly into the great rivers and seas.

title: 辩德
original: 知人者智，自知者明。胜人者有力，自胜者强。知足者富。强行者有志。不失其所者久。死而不亡者，寿。
translation: He who knows well the merits and demerits of other people is merely intelligent; He who knows his own nature thoroughly is truly wise. He who is able to overcome others is powerful; Yet he who is able to overcome his own weaknesses proves a man of real strength. Being content with what he has is to be blessed with wealth; He who follows the Tao and perseveres in acting accordingly is a strong-willed man; He who bases his life on the Tao and clings to it his whole life is a man who endures; He who passes away, yet whose spirit embodying the Tao remains for good will enjoy true longevity.
commentaryZh: 本章主要论述个人修养的层次与境界问题，围绕“智、明、力、强、富、志、久、 寿”八个字展开论述，其核心思想是“人贵有自知之明”。《孙子兵法》中的“知己知彼，百战不殆”与其内核相通。了解别人的长处和短处的人算是聪明的，而能真正了解自己的人才是高明的；能够战胜别人的人是刚强有力的，但能“知其雄，守其雌”并战胜自己弱点的人才是不可战胜的。懂得知足的人是富有的，因为他不贪婪。为既定的人生目标坚持不懈、持之以恒而努力的人是有志向的。 一生始终不脱离根本，依“道”而行的人就会长久不衰。肉体消亡了，但其体现 “道”的那种精神却永存人间，这样的人才是真正长寿的。
commentaryEn: This chapter mainly discusses the levels and realms of personal cultivation. Its discussion centers on eight key ideas: intelligence, wisdom, power, strength, power, wealth, willpower, endurance, and longevity. The core message is that one should possess true self-awareness. This echoes with the well-known saying in the Art of War—“Know the enemy and know yourself, and you can fight a hundred battles with no danger of defeat”. Those who understand the strengths and weaknesses of others may be considered intelligent, but those who truly understand themselves are truly wise. Those who defeat others may be regarded as strong and powerful, yet those who are able to “know the masculine yet keep to the feminine” and overcome their own weaknesses possess true strength. Those who know contentment are truly wealthy, because they are free from greed. Those who persist tirelessly toward their life goals are people of strong willpower. A person who acts in accordance with the Tao his whole life will endure. Although his physical body may perish, the spirit that embodies the Tao will remain forever. Only such a person can possess true longevity.

title: 任成
original: 大道泛兮，其可左右。万物恃之以生而不辞，功成而不名有。衣养万物而不为主，常无欲可名於小。万物归焉，而不为主，可名为大。以其终不自为大，故能成其大。
translation: The Great Tao overflows far and wide, extending in all directions. All things depend on it for life, yet it never rejects them; It accomplishes much, yet never claims credit for that. It nurtures the myriad things without claiming to be their head, which can be called “Small"; The myriad things eventually return to it, yet it never claims to be their master, which can be called “Great'".
