translation: One who knows the Tao but does not think he knows it is the best man; One who does not know the Tao but claims that he knows it is a man of definite defect. The sage is free from this defect because he recognizes such a defect as a defect. Therefore: Because the sage considers this defect as a defect, he is immune to such a defect.
commentaryZh: 本章读起来有点像绕口令。老子指出：有道的圣人因为有自知之明，从而避免了犯自以为是的错误，而俗人因无自知之明，所以总是自以为是而导致不断犯错误。孔子在《论语》（为政篇）说：“知之为知之，不知为不知，是知也。”孔子此句的含义与老子本章所论述的内容有异曲同工之妙。
commentaryEn: This chapter reads almost like a tongue-twister. Laozi contrasts the sage, whose self-knowledge guards him against self-righteousness, with ordinary people, who lack such awareness and therefore persist in the belief that they are always right. A similar idea appears in The Analects, where Confucius remarks: “Wisdom lies in admitting what know as well as what you don’t know.” Though expressed differently, Confucius’s insight resonates closely with Laozi’s argument in this chapter.

title: 爱己
original: 民不畏威，则大威至。无狎其所居，无厌其所生。夫唯不厌，是以不厌。是以圣人自知不自见。自爱不自贵。故去彼取此。
translation: If the people no longer fear the tyranny of a tyrant, a great revolt will soon arise.A ruler should in no way harass their living places; He should in no way deprive them of their livelihood. If a ruler chooses not to oppress his people, they will not resent him. Therefore: The sage should know himself and choose not to praise himself; He should discipline himself and choose not to glorify himself. Therefore: He should take the former and reject the latter.
commentaryZh: 在本章中，老子旗帜鲜明地警告统治者必须“自知”不能“自见”，要“自爱”不要“自贵”,不然一定会遭到人民的反抗并被推翻统治。老子说当百姓不再畏惧统治者的权威、暴政及恐怖的国家机器的时候，那么更大的祸乱就要来临了，因为人民揭竿而起来推翻其残暴统治的时刻就要到了。不要压缩人民的生存空间使他们不得安居，不要压制他们的谋生出路使他们不得谋生。如果统治者能够不去压制人民的谋生之路，那么百姓也不会厌恶他们的统治者。所以，有道的圣人有自知之明而不自以为是、自我炫耀，自我尊重而不自以为比百姓高贵。因此，统治者应该“自知”“自爱”而不是“自见”“自贵”，这样才能成为受百姓拥护的君王。
commentaryEn: In this chapter, Laozi warns rulers clearly that they must know themselves rather than boast about themselves, and discipline themselves rather than glorify themselves. Otherwise, rebellion and the collapse of their rule will be inevitable. Laozi observes that when people no longer fear the regime’s reliance on coercion and terror, greater turmoil is sure to follow—for this signals the moment of rebellion. Rulers must not constrict the people’s living space or block their means of livelihood, leaving them unable to survive. When rulers refrain from doing so, the people, in turn, will not resent their rulers. Laozi therefore concludes that only those who practice self-knowledge and self-restraint, rather than self-promotion and self-exaltation, can earn the lasting support of the people.

title: 任为
original: 勇於敢则杀。勇於不敢则活。此两者或利或害。天之所恶孰知其故。天之道不争而善胜。不言而善应。不召而自来。繟(chǎn,舒缓)然而善谋。天网恢恢疏而不失。
translation: One whose bravery lies in boldness will surely perish; One whose bravery lies in pliancy will survive. These are two sorts of bravery, in which the former proves harmful and the latter beneficial. Who knows why the Tao of Heaven hates what it detests? Even the sage finds it hard to understand. The Tao of Heaven is good at winning without contending; It responds readily without speaking; It attracts all things without calling; It is at ease and plans well. The Tao of Heaven resembles a giant net, extending everywhere; Its meshes are big and wide, yet nothing can slip through them.
commentaryZh: 在本章中，老子论述了两种“勇”（守柔卑下的勇和逞强好胜的勇）及其带来的不同结局。前者可以保命，而后者让人丧命。两种勇一个得利，一个招致灾难。天道所厌恶的事情，谁能明白为什么呢？有道的圣人也感到很难理解此 因。天道的规律是“反”的。不争却常常取胜，不说话却善于回应，不命令却主 动来归，悠哉坦然而善于谋划。天道的规律无处不在，涵盖万物。天道的法网 看似稀疏，但没有什么东西能从它的网眼中逃脱。
commentaryEn: In this chapter, Laozi contrasts two kinds of courage: one grounded in gentleness, the other in boldness. The first preserves life and brings benefit; the second invites disaster and destruction . What the Tao of Heaven rejects is often hard to grasp—even sages find it confusing. The Tao of Heaven works through paradox. It does not contend, yet it prevails; it does not speak, yet it answers; it does not command, yet all things return to it naturally. Unhurried and at ease, it plans well. The Tao of Heaven pervades all things. Its net may appear loose, but nothing ever escapes it.

title: 制惑
original: 民不畏死，奈何以死惧之。若使民常畏死，而为奇者，吾得执而杀之，孰敢。常有司杀者杀。夫代司杀者杀，是谓代大匠斫。夫代大匠斫者，希有不伤其手矣。
translation: If the people do not fear death, what's the use of threatening them with it?If a ruler intends to make his people fear death, the best way is to arrest and kill the criminal who commits serious crimes; In this way the people will shrink from doing evils. The Tao of Heaven always functions as a judge of life and death. No tyrant is needed to kill those evildoers. A tyrant who presumes to kill on behalf of the Tao of Heaven is like chopping wood on behalf of a master carpenter. Any tyrant who kills by replacing the Tao of Heaven seldom avoids being harmed.
commentaryZh: 在本章中，老子呼吁统治者要珍爱百姓的生命，不要乱杀无辜，这体现了他的人道主义思想。老子认为统治者不依道而行，为满足自己的私欲而妄为，导致百姓无法生存，只能揭竿而起为生存一搏。统治者不但没有用合适的方式改善天下百姓的生存状态，反而用高压、严刑峻法、国家机器等手段来镇压、恐吓百姓，其结果是百姓不再怕死。老子认为要使百姓畏惧死亡，最好的办法是把做坏事的人抓起来杀掉，那就没有人敢做坏事了。天道是主宰人生死的最高裁判。代替专门管杀人的人去杀人，就好像是代替手艺高明的木匠去砍木材。这 种代替高明木匠去砍木材的人，很少会有不伤到自己手的。老子在这里委婉地指出统治者就是代替高明的木匠（天道）来行生杀大权的人，他们最终也将伤害到自己（政权被推翻）。
commentaryEn: In this chapter, Laozi urges rulers to cherish human life and not to slaughter the innocent, revealing his humanitarian concern. He argues that when rulers act against the Tao to satisfy their own desires, they reduce their people’s life to misery, leaving them no choice but to rebel. Instead of improving people’s conditions, such rulers rely on severe punishments and laws to suppress and intimidate them. The result is that people lose their fear of death altogether. Laozi observes that if one wishes to make people fear death, the proper approach is to kill those who commit crimes. Yet it is the Tao of Heaven that is the highest judge of all beings. To kill in place of this higher order is like cutting wood in place of a master carpenter: those who presume to wield such power are likely to injure themselves. In this way, Laozi indicates that rulers who kill on behalf of the Tao will ultimately bring harm upon themselves—often in the form of the collapse of their own governance.

title: 贪损
original: 民之饥以其上食税之多，是以饥。民之难治以其上之有为，是以难治。民之轻死以其求生之厚，是以轻死。夫唯无以生为者，是贤於贵生。
translation: The people often suffer from starvation because heavy taxes are imposed upon them. The people are hard to cope with because rulers often interfere too much with their affairs. The people take death lightly because rulers pursue a lavishly extravagant life.A ruler who practices non-action, serving his people heart and soul, does far better than the one who holds dearer his own life.
commentaryZh: 在本章中，老子再一次旗帜鲜明地警告统治者不要把百姓逼上绝路，不然百姓揭竿造反将成为必然。老百姓挨饿的原因就是统治者苛捐杂税多如牛毛；老百姓难以治理就是因为统治者欲壑难平、肆意妄为（作为太多）。统治者搜刮民脂民膏过度，民不聊生，所以百姓轻生反抗、冒死一搏。有道的圣人（统治者）摈弃自己的私欲、不看重个人享乐、全心全意为百姓服务，这样的统治者要胜过纵欲奢侈的那些所谓“贵生”的统治者。
commentaryEn: In this chapter, Laozi warns rulers not to push their people to the brink of despair, for rebellion then becomes inevitable. People suffer from hunger because of heavy taxes; they are difficult to govern because rulers desire too much and interfere too much with their people’s affairs. When oppression reduces people to misery, people are forced to rebel, even at the risk of their lives. In contrast, a sage or a ruler following the Tao sets aside personal desires and serves his people wholeheartedly. Such a ruler is better than those who prioritize themselves over their people.

title: 戒强
original: 人之生也柔弱，其死也坚强。草木之生也柔脆，其死也枯槁。故坚强者死之徒，柔弱者生之徒。是以兵强则灭，木强则折。强大处下，柔弱处上。
translation: When a man is alive, his body remains soft and supple; But when he is dead, his body becomes hard and stiff. When plants are alive, they also remain soft and supple; But when they are dead, they become dry and brittle. Therefore: Stiff and hard things belong to the dead; Soft and supple things belong to the living. For this reason, a strong and arbitrary army is doomed to failure, and a strong and grown tree will be cut down sooner or later. The hard and strong things are inferior to the soft and supple things.
commentaryZh: 在本章中，老子论述了他著名的“柔弱胜刚强”的思想，即“贵柔守柔”的思 想。老子通过对事物细致入微的观察认识到：凡是柔弱的存在都属于生的范 畴，但凡刚强的存在都属于死的范畴。人活着的时候，身体是柔软灵活的，而死 亡的时候身体就僵硬笔直了。草木活着时柔软脆弱，可死了的时候就变得干枯 易断。所以，坚硬刚强的属于死亡范畴，而柔软脆弱的属于生命范畴。因此，用 兵逞强好胜就会失败乃至灭亡，树木长得强硬、高大就会被风折断或被砍伐。 所以，强大的事物往往处于劣势，而柔弱的事物则往往处于优势。
commentaryEn: In this chapter, Laozi expounds his well-known teaching that “the soft and the yielding overcome the hard and the strong,” emphasizing the principle of valuing and preserving softness. Through careful observation of natural phenomena, Laozi recognized that all soft and flexible forms belong to the category of life, whereas all rigid and unyielding forms belong to the category of death. When a person is alive, the body is supple and soft; when death occurs, the body becomes stiff and hard. Plants and trees, while living, are soft and supple, yet once they die, they become dry and brittle. Therefore, what is hard and rigid belongs to the realm of death, whereas what is soft and yielding belongs to the realm of life. For this reason, an army that relies on forceful aggression and the pursuit of victory is likely to suffer defeat and even destruction, just as trees that grow excessively hard and tall are easily broken by the wind or cut down. Thus, whatever appears strong often occupies a vulnerable position, whereas whatever appears soft often possesses the advantage.

title: 天道
original: 天之道其犹张弓与。高者抑之，下者举之。有馀者损之，不足者补之。天之道，损有馀而补不足。人之道，则不然，损不足以奉有馀。孰能有馀以奉天下，唯有道者。是以圣人为而不恃，功成而不处。其不欲见贤邪！
translation: Isn't the Tao of Heaven like a drawn bow? If the bow is a little high, one can lower it; If it is a little low, one can raise it; If the string is a little long, one can shorten it; If the string is a little short, one can lengthen it. It is the Tao of Heaven to reduce surplus to supplement insufficiency. But the Tao of man is just opposite: reducing insuffi ciency to supplement surplus. Who can reduce surplus to supplement insufficiency? Only the sage can do that. Therefore: The sage accomplishes things, but does not claim his ownership; He contributes much, but claims no credit for that; He does this because he has no wish to be called "superior"
commentaryZh: 在本章中，老子提出了他著名的“天之道，损有余而补不足”和“人之道，损不足以奉有余”的思想。他认为只有得道的圣人（统治者）才能做到“有余以奉天下”，即只有圣人才能调整“人道”并向“天道”看齐。得道的圣人有所作为但不居功自傲和仗恃己力，他不愿意炫耀自己的过人之处。
commentaryEn: In this chapter, Laozi distinguishes “the Tao of Heaven” from “the Tao of man”. The Tao of Heaven is to reduces the surplus to supplement the deficient, while the Tao of man is just the opposite: reducing insufficiency to supplement surplus He argues that only a sage who follows the Tao can practice the Tao of Heaven to “reduce surplus to supplement insufficiency”. Such a sage accomplishes much, yet never claims credit or relies on personal power, for he is unwilling to boast about his extraordinary talents.

title: 任信
original: 天下莫柔弱於水。而攻坚强者，莫之能胜。以其无以易之。弱之胜强。柔之胜刚。天下莫不知莫能行。是以圣人云，受国之垢是谓社稷主。受国不祥是为天下王。正言若反。
translation: Nothing in the world is weaker than water, but when it comes to attacking the hard and the strong, nothing can do better than it. Why is this? Because nothing can replace it. The weak can overcome the strong; The soft can conquer the hard; This truth is well-known to the world, but few people are able to put it into practice. Therefore: The sage remarks, "Only the man who can bear the disgraces and disasters on behalf of his country is qualified to be its head. " More often than not, such truthful words sound paradoxical.
commentaryZh: 在本章中，老子再次以水为例进一步阐释他的“以柔克刚”的哲学思想。老子认为天下万事万物没有比水更柔弱的了，但用于攻克坚强、坚硬的东西时，却没有什么东西能胜过水，因为没有任何东西可以替代它。弱小的东西可以战胜强大的东西，柔弱的东西可以攻克刚强的东西。天下没有人不懂得这个道理，却很少有人能践行它。所以，有道的圣人说：能够为国家承受耻辱的人，才配当国家的君主；能为天下承受灾难的人，才配当天下的君王。老子认为有道的君王应具备“水德”，即懂得谦卑处下、处众人之所恶、利他而不争。老子说能体现 “道”的言语往往听起来像反话
commentaryEn: In this chapter, Laozi once again uses water as an example to illustrate his thinking of “overcoming the strong through softness.” He observes that nothing in the world is softer than water, yet nothing can do better than it when attacking strong and hard things, for nothing can take its place. The weak can overcome the strong; the soft can prevail over the hard. Everyone in the world understands this, yet few are able to put it into practice. For this reason, the sage says that only the person who can bear disgrace and disasters for the sake of the state is fit to be its ruler. Laozi maintains that a ruler who follows the Tao should behave like water: humble and willing to stay in lowly positions that others detest, and willing to benefit others without expecting reward. He also notes that these words which truly accord with the Tao often sound paradoxical.

title: 任契
original: 和大怨必有馀怨，安可以为善。是以圣人执左契，而不责於人。有德司契，无德司彻。天道无亲常与善人。
translation: With a great resentment reconciled, some grudge will surely linger behind;Even if one repays hostility with kindness, how can that be deemed as a proper solution? Therefore: The sage always keeps the receipt but never demands its payment. The virtuous man gives, but does not take; The vicious man exacts the payment like a harsh tax collector. The Tao of Heaven is impartial, favoring only those who follow it.
commentaryZh: 在本章中，老子再一次旗帜鲜明地警告统治者要避免与百姓产生不可调和的激烈矛盾，不要因为自己的妄为而积怨于民。如果仇恨过深就很难化解，即使积怨得到调和或以德报怨（即使君主以德报怨），但小怨必定挥之不去，所以这不算是解决问题的好办法啊！所以，有道的圣人（统治者）一定是手拿着借据的存根而不去强行向借债人（百姓）催讨。有德的管理者（统治者）保留借据但从不催债，而无德的管理者（统治者）如同掌管税收的官员那样苛刻，毫无怜悯之心，不停地向百姓索取和催逼。天道规律没有偏私之情，无亲无疏，但总是帮助和眷顾那些依道而行的人们，正所谓：顺天者昌，逆天者亡。
commentaryEn: In this chapter, Laozi once again warned that rulers should avoid serious conflicts with their people for bad governance. Even if a great resentment is reconciled or eased by the ruler’s virtue, some grudge will surely linger. Therefore, this is no good solution to serious grudge. Thus, even with a receipt, the sage or the ruler who follows the Tao never press their people for repayment. That is what a virtuous ruler will do, whereas a vicious ruler exacts without any sympathy, just like a harsh tax collector. The Tao of Heaven is impartial, yet it helps those who act in accordance with it. As the saying goes, those who follow Heaven prosper, while those who go against it decline.

title: 独立
original: 小国寡民。使有什伯之器而不用。使民重死而不远徙。虽有舟舆无所乘之。虽有甲兵无所陈之。使民复结绳而用之。甘其食、美其服、安其居、乐其俗。邻国相望，鸡犬之声相闻。民至老死不相往来。
translation: An ideal country is like the following: It should be a small country with a small population. In such a country no tyranny prevails; Much as all kinds of tools are available, they remain unused; The people have no need to make a living far away from home, risking losing their lives; Much as there are boats and carriages, they are no longer in need; Much as all sorts of weapons are available, there is no need to display them. The people return to the old way of using knots to record things. They eat plain food, but they enjoy it; They wear coarse clothes, but they find them beautiful; They live in humble dwellings, but they find them comfortable; They delight in their customs, though they are simple. The people of the neighboring countries can see each other, hear their dogs and cocks, but they never visit each other till they die.
commentaryZh: 在本章中，老子描述了他心向往之的“理想国”。这是个国小人少的国家，人们过着恬淡安逸的生活。这里民风淳朴，相邻国家之间没有冲突和战争，仿佛一幅世外桃源的景象。人们虽有各种各样的工具但不使用；在这样的国家，人们看重死亡而不会背井离乡去远方讨生活；虽然有车船，但没有使用它们的必要；虽有武器装备，但没地方陈列；百姓又回归到结绳记事的简单生活方式了。他们觉得自己的食物吃起来很香，自己的衣服穿起来很漂亮，自己的居所住起来很舒服，他们热衷于自己的文化习俗。邻国之间没有冲突和纷争，鸡犬之声相闻,因为人们生活俭朴，需求极少，没有贸易和发动战争的必要，邻国之间互不侵犯，所以百姓至死也不来往。
commentaryEn: In this chapter, Laozi depicts an “ideal state”. It is a small country with a small population, where people live calm and contented lives. Social customs are simple and there are no conflicts or wars between neighboring states, which creates a scene of utopia. Though there are all sorts of tools, there is no need to use them. People do not risk their lives for making a living far from home. Though there are boats and carriages, there is no need to travel by them; though there are weapons, there is no need to display them. People return to a simple way of life, even to the practice of knot-tying in place of written records. They find their food flavorful, their clothing pleasing, their dwellings comfortable, and they take satisfaction in their own simple customs. Neighboring states live within sight and hearing of one another, yet there is no trade or warfare because people live frugally and desire little. Thus the people live out their lives without ever traveling beyond their borders.

title: 显质
original: 信言不美。美言不信。善者不辩。辩者不善。知者不博。博者不知。圣人不积。既以为人己愈有。既以与人己愈多。天之道利而不害。圣人之道为而不争。
translation: Truthful and sincere words do not often sound pleasant to ears; Beautiful words may not necessarily be true and sincere. A man who knows the Tao does not justify himself; A man who tries to justify himself does not know the Tao. A man who knows the Tao does not necessarily know much; A man who knows much does not necessarily know the Tao. The sage lives for others; The more he helps others, the more he gains; The more he gives others, the more he accumulates. The Tao of Heaven benefits all things but does them no harm; The sage follows the Tao of Heaven: he acts to benefit people but claims no credit for that.
commentaryZh: 在本章中，老子总结性地概括了“天之道”是“利而不害”和“圣人之道”是 “为而不争”。该思想是贯穿《道德经》的核心思想之一，是君王治世的最高准则，也是人生追求的最高境界。老子辩证地论述：诚实不欺的话听起来不悦耳，花言巧语好听但虚伪不实在。依道而行的人不巧言争辩，狡辩的人不依道而行。有道的人不一定知识广博，而知识广博的人未必是有道之人。有道的圣人不积攒财富，不让私欲控制自己，越是帮助别人越感觉自己富有，给予别人的越多自己拥有的就越多。天道就是利万物而不伤害它们；圣人的原则是多做利他的事而不去争功。
commentaryEn: In this chapter, Laozi concludes that the “Tao of Heaven” is to benefit without causing harm, while the sage is to act without claiming credit. This thought is one of the core principles of Taoism, and it serves as the highest guideline for governance and a meaningful life. Laozi argues that true and sincere words may not sound pleasant, while beautiful words can be deceitful and hollow. Those who follow the Tao avoid justifying for themselves, while those who do not follow the Tao do the opposite. A person who follows the Tao doesn’t necessarily possess much knowledge, and someone with much knowledge doesn’t necessarily know the Tao. Guided by the Tao, the sage is not obsessed with wealth or other desires. On the opposite, the more he helps others, the richer he becomes; the more he gives, the more he possesses. The Tao of Heaven nurtures all things without harming them, and the sage benefits others without seeking recognition or reward.
